title: 7  Social choice and voting
text:
7.1 Constitutions
Chapter 1 showed that a single rational decision maker has a utility function. Can a group of rational individuals be summarised by a rational collective preference? The question matters well beyond elections: scheduling packets under several criteria, choosing among solutions of a multi-objective optimisation, or allocating resources by competing priorities are all “votes”. The answer, in the form of Arrow’s impossibility theorem, is essentially negative, and the paradoxes of voting systems show why.
Let \(\mathcal R(A)\) be the set of rational preferences on a set of alternatives \(A\), and let \(n\) individuals have preferences \((\succeq_1, \dots, \succeq_n)\), a profile.
crumbs: Part II: Static games of complete information

title: 7  Social choice and voting
text:
A constitution (social welfare function) is a map \(f : \mathcal R(A)^n \to \mathcal R(A)\) turning every profile into a social preference \(\succeq = f(\succeq_1, \dots, \succeq_n)\). For \(Y \subseteq A\), \(\succeq|_Y = \succeq \cap (Y \times Y)\) denotes the restriction to \(Y\).



Independence of irrelevant alternatives (IIA): if two profiles agree on the pair \(\{a, b\}\) for every individual, the social preferences agree on \(\{a, b\}\). Adding or removing other alternatives does not change how society ranks \(a\) against \(b\).
Pareto efficiency: if \(a \succeq_i b\) for every \(i\), then \(a \succeq b\).
Dictatorship: there is an individual \(i\) such that \(a \succeq_i b\) implies \(a \succeq b\) for every profile.
Monotonicity: if one individual raises an alternative in their ranking, society does not rank it lower.
Non-imposition: every rational preference is the output of some profile (\(f\) is surjective).



With at least three alternatives, no constitution is simultaneously non-dictatorial, monotonic, IIA and non-imposed. Equivalently (1963 version): every Pareto-efficient constitution satisfying IIA is a dictatorship.

title: 7  Social choice and voting
text:
7.5 Ways out
No universally good system exists, but there are escape routes:

Weaken the axioms (e.g. drop IIA, as Borda does).
Restrict the domain of admissible profiles. Majority rule, \(a \succeq b \iff |\{i : a \succeq_i b\}| \geq |\{i : b \succeq_i a\}|\), is Pareto efficient, IIA and non-dictatorial, but in general not transitive because of Condorcet cycles — so it is not a constitution. On domains where cycles cannot occur it becomes one: Black (1948) showed this for single-peaked preferences (alternatives on a line, each voter preferring options closer to their ideal point), Sen (1966) gave more general conditions.
Change the ballot: approval voting with free choice of \(N\), or voting “for” and “against”.







For engineering, the lesson is that aggregating several performance criteria into a single ranking is never neutral. Every scalarisation (weighted sums are Borda-like) embodies choices that can reverse rankings when an irrelevant option is added or removed.

title: 7  Social choice and voting
text:
7.6 Voting as a game
An election can itself be modelled as a static game: voters are players, ballots are strategies, and the rule maps profiles to outcomes. Three observations follow.

Two candidates: voting sincerely is weakly dominant, since your ballot matters only when it is pivotal, and then you want your favourite to win. The median voter result of Chapter 4 describes the candidates’ side of this game.
Three or more candidates: sincere voting is generally not an equilibrium. Under plurality, supporters of a hopeless candidate prefer to vote for the lesser evil among the front-runners, which is why plurality systems tend to two parties (Duverger’s law). Run-off systems invite subtler manipulation: supporting a weak opponent in the first round to meet them in the second.
Equilibrium is too permissive: with many voters no single ballot is pivotal, so every profile in which a candidate wins by two or more votes is a Nash equilibrium, including everyone voting for their least favourite. One must first delete weakly dominated ballots, or study coalitions of like-minded voters, as in the exercises.

The Gibbard–Satterthwaite theorem guarantees that some profile always rewards misreporting. The useful question for a given rule is therefore who can manipulate, and whether the others can counter it. A Condorcet winner, when it exists, is robust: any coalition preferring another candidate is a minority in the head-to-head comparison.

title: 7  Social choice and voting
text:
7.7 Exercises
Problems from Badia and Marchioro (BM), Chapter 4.

(BM 4.8) Thirteen students elect a class representative by plurality among A, B, C. Preferences: students 1–5: \(A \succ B \succ C\); 6–9: \(B \succ C \succ A\); 10–12: \(C \succ B \succ A\); 13: \(C \succ A \succ B\). (a) Who wins with sincere voting? (b) How can students 10–12 manipulate the result? (c) Can A’s supporters counter?


Solution. 

A \(5\), B \(4\), C \(4\): A wins. (b) Students 10–12 prefer B to A: voting B gives B \(7\) votes and B wins. (c) A’s supporters could only block B by voting C, which would at best tie and which they dislike more than B. They have no counter. B is the Condorcet winner (B beats A \(7\)–\(6\) and C \(9\)–\(4\)), so the manipulation actually restores the majority’s choice.



(BM 4.9) A two-round run-off among A (42%, \(B \succ C \succ D\) after A), B (11%, \(A \succ C \succ D\)), C (27%, \(B \succ D \succ A\)), D (20%, \(C \succ B \succ A\)). (a) Sincere outcome? (b) Best strategic vote for D’s supporters? (c) Who wins then, and can A’s supporters respond?


Solution. 

A and C reach the ballot; B’s voters prefer A, so A wins \(53\)–\(47\). (b) D’s supporters prefer B to A: voting B in round one sends A and B to the ballot (B \(31\%\), C \(27\%\)). (c) B wins the ballot with \(58\%\) (everyone but A’s supporters): B is the Condorcet winner despite the fewest first preferences. A’s supporters cannot beat B head-to-head, so they must keep B out of the ballot. If \(7\) of their \(42\) points vote C in round one (A \(35\), C \(34\), B \(31\)), A meets C again and wins \(53\)–\(47\). Manipulation invites counter-manipulation, and the outcome depends on who coordinates better.


From the course material:

Verify that in the instant run-off example the two voters who switch to \(A > B > C\) cause \(A\) to lose, and compute the Condorcet winner (if any) in both profiles.


Solution. Original: first places \(A\) 6, \(C\) 5, \(B\) 6 → \(C\) out, its 5 votes go to \(A\) → \(A\) 11. Pairwise: \(A\) vs \(B\): \(6 + 5 = 11\) prefer \(A\); \(A\) vs \(C\): \(6 + 2 = 8\) prefer \(A\) vs \(9\) prefer \(C\), so \(C\) beats \(A\); \(B\) vs \(C\): \(6+4+2=12\) prefer \(B\). \(B > C > A\) and \(A > B\): a cycle, no Condorcet winner. Modified profile: first places \(A\) 8, \(C\) 5, \(B\) 4 → \(B\) out, its 4 votes go to \(C\) → \(C\) 9 beats \(A\) 8. Pairwise: \(A > B\) (13–4), \(C > A\) (9–8), \(B > C\) (12–5): again a cycle.


Show that majority rule over three alternatives is transitive whenever all voters’ preferences are single-peaked on the order \(A < B < C\).


Solution. Single-peakedness on \(A<B<C\) forbids \(B\) being ranked last, leaving the orders \(ABC\), \(BAC\), \(BCA\), \(CBA\). A cycle \(A > B > C > A\) would need a strict majority with \(A\) over \(B\) (only \(ABC\) voters) and a strict majority with \(C\) over \(A\) (only \(BCA\), \(CBA\) voters): two disjoint groups, each larger than \(n/2\) — impossible. The reverse cycle \(A > C > B > A\) needs a majority with \(C\) over \(B\) (only \(CBA\)) and one with \(A\) over \(C\) (\(ABC\), \(BAC\)), again disjoint. Hence no cycle exists and majority rule is transitive; in fact the median voter’s ranking decides every pairwise contest.

title: 8  Extensive-form games
text:
8.1 Dynamic games
In many interactions some players move first and others react. The bi-matrix hides this time structure, so we need a richer representation: the extensive form, a game tree annotated with who moves where and what they know. This chapter introduces the tree, information sets, the redefinition of strategy as a complete contingent plan, behavioural strategies, and the correspondence between extensive and normal forms.
A dynamic game has players moving at different times. Complete information is kept — payoffs are common knowledge — but a new distinction appears:
The sequential Battle of the Sexes. In the static version Ann and Brian choose without knowing each other’s choice — not very realistic. Suppose instead Ann picks the movie first and phones Brian. Being fully informed, Ann knows that whatever she picks, Brian’s best response is to follow; since she prefers R, she picks R. There is no coordination problem any more. To represent this we need to connect each choice to the knowledge available when it is made — Brian’s call might not go through, for example.

title: 8  Extensive-form games
text:
8.3 Information sets
Label nodes \(x_0\) (the root), \(x_1, x_2, \dots\); each node is either terminal (carrying payoffs) or the parent of other nodes. In the sequential Battle of the Sexes, Brian moves at \(x_1\) (after \(R\)) or \(x_2\) (after \(S\)) with the same actions but different consequences — and he knows which node he is at.

Each player \(i\) has a collection \(H_i\) of information sets. The information set \(h_i(x) \in H_i\) associated with a node \(x\) where \(i\) moves contains all nodes that \(i\) cannot distinguish from \(x\); by convention \(x \in h_i(x)\). If \(h_i(x) = \{x\}\) is a singleton, \(i\) knows exactly where they are. All nodes in the same information set must have the same set of available actions: \(x' \in h_i(x) \Rightarrow A(x') = A(x)\).

In the simultaneous Battle of the Sexes, Brian’s information set is \(\{x_1, x_2\}\): he does not know Ann’s choice. Graphically, nodes in the same set are joined by a dashed line (or enclosed in an oval).

Remark (Equalising action sets). If two indistinguishable nodes seem to offer different actions, add “forbidden” actions with payoff \(-M\), where \(M\) is huge (formally \(-\infty\), or below the minimum payoff). The game changes, but every strategy using the forbidden action becomes strictly dominated, so nothing of substance is altered.


A dynamic game has perfect information if all information sets are singletons and Nature never moves. Otherwise it has imperfect information: either exogenous uncertainty (Nature’s moves, as in single-person problems with lotteries) or endogenous uncertainty (unobserved, effectively simultaneous moves of other players). In both cases players must form beliefs.

title: 8  Extensive-form games
text:
8.4 Strategies in dynamic games
In static games a pure strategy is an action. In dynamic games the history matters through information sets.

A pure strategy of player \(i\) specifies an action at every information set of \(i\) — including those that will not be reached given the strategy itself. It is a complete program: a countermove for every possible situation.

In the sequential Battle of the Sexes Brian has two actions but four strategies, written \((a_R, a_S)\) = (reply to \(R\), reply to \(S\)): \((s,s)\) “go to S no matter what”, \((r,r)\) “go to R no matter what”, \((r,s)\) “do what Ann does”, \((s,r)\) “avoid Ann”.
If the static Battle of the Sexes is played on two consecutive nights with the first outcome observed, a strategy is a quintuple \((a_1, a_{2}^{Rr}, a_{2}^{Rs}, a_{2}^{Sr}, a_{2}^{Ss})\): the first-night move and the second-night reply to each of the four possible first-night outcomes. For instance \((r, s, r, r, r)\) means “R on the first night; S on the second if the first outcome was \(Rr\), otherwise R”. The count explodes quickly: two sequential moves with \(|A_1| = |A_2| = 3\) already give player 2 \(3^3 = 27\) strategies. Beyond small examples strategies are described implicitly.

title: 8  Extensive-form games
text:
8.5 Mixed and behavioural strategies
A mixed strategy is still a probability distribution over the (now large) set of pure strategies: the randomisation happens once, at the start, and the player then sticks to the drawn plan. Alternatively, a player can randomise as the game unfolds.

A behavioural strategy of player \(i\) specifies, for each information set \(h_i \in H_i\), an independent probability distribution \(\sigma_i(\cdot \mid h_i)\) over the actions \(A_i(h_i)\) available there.

Think of a strategy as a handbook of instructions. A mixed strategy picks one of several handbooks at random; a behavioural strategy is a single handbook whose every page gives a random instruction. In the sequential Battle of the Sexes, a mixed strategy of Brian assigns \(p_{rr}, p_{rs}, p_{sr}, p_{ss}\); the equivalent behavioural strategy has \[\sigma_B(r \mid x_1) = p_{rr} + p_{rs}, \qquad \sigma_B(r \mid x_2) = p_{rr} + p_{sr}.\]

In a finite game with perfect recall — no player ever forgets information they previously knew, including their own past actions — every mixed strategy has an outcome-equivalent behavioural strategy and vice versa.

Perfect recall holds in virtually every game of interest. When it fails, the two notions can differ.

Andrew drives home on a highway at night. Exiting at the first junction leads into a bad neighbourhood (payoff \(0\)); exiting at the second takes him home (payoff \(4\)); missing both leads to a long detour (payoff \(1\)). Andrew is tired and cannot tell the two junctions apart: his single information set is \(\{x_0, x_1\}\), so the same action must be chosen at both.

Pure and mixed strategies. “Exit” gives \(0\), “continue” gives \(1\); any mixture yields at most \(1\).
Behavioural strategy. Exit with probability \(p\) at each junction, independently: \[\mathbb E[u] = p \cdot 0 + (1-p)p \cdot 4 + (1-p)^2 \cdot 1 = -3p^2 + 2p + 1,\] maximised at \(p^* = \tfrac13\) with \(\mathbb E[u] = \tfrac43 > 1\).

Randomising at each node beats every mixture over plans. A further paradox appears at the action stage: if Andrew believes he is at the first junction with probability \(q\), the expected payoff becomes \(-3qp^2 - qp + 3p + 1\), whose maximiser equals the planning-stage \(p^* = \tfrac13\) only when \(q = 1\).

title: 8  Extensive-form games
section: 8.7 How large is the normal form?
text:
8.7 How large is the normal form?
A pure strategy specifies an action at every information set of the player, reached or not. If player \(i\) has information sets \(h_1, \dots, h_K\) with \(|A(h_k)|\) actions each, then \[|S_i| = \prod_{k=1}^K |A(h_k)|,\] which explodes with the depth of the tree. In a game where player 2 answers each of player 1’s three moves with \(S\) or \(N\), player 2 has \(2^3 = 8\) strategies, even though only one answer is ever used.
Two simplifications are standard:

Reduced normal form. Strategies that differ only at information sets made unreachable by the player’s own earlier moves are payoff-equivalent and can be merged. A player who ends the game at the root need not say what they would do later. Many textbooks still list them, because subgame perfection does care about those plans.
Simultaneous moves inside a tree. Moves made without observing each other are drawn in any order, with the later mover’s nodes joined in one information set. The choice of who is drawn first is cosmetic.

The normal form is the right tool for finding all Nash equilibria, including those supported by unreasonable plans off the path of play. The extensive form is the right tool for discarding them (Chapter 9).

title: 8  Extensive-form games
text:
8.8 Exercises
Problems from Badia and Marchioro (BM), Chapters 3 and 4. Their subgame-perfect equilibria are found in Chapter 9.

(BM 3.1) A student U chooses project quality \(x \in \{0, 1, 2\}\); the professor P then accepts (S) or rejects (N). If accepted, each gets \(m - e_j\) with mark \(m = 18 + 6x\), \(e_U = 4^x\) and \(e_P = 15\); a rejection gives \(0\) to both. Draw the tree, write the normal form and find all pure NE.


Solution. Accepted payoffs (U, P): \(x = 0\): \((17, 3)\); \(x = 1\): \((20, 9)\); \(x = 2\): \((14, 15)\). P has one information set per \(x\), hence \(2^3 = 8\) strategies (an answer to \(0\), \(1\) and \(2\)). The normal form is \(3 \times 8\); marking best responses gives 7 pure NE: \((0, SNS)\), \((0, SNN)\), \((1, SSS)\), \((1, SSN)\), \((1, NSS)\), \((1, NSN)\), \((2, NNS)\). Several rely on P rejecting projects that are never submitted. \((2, NNS)\), for instance, is the “strict professor” who accepts only top quality.


(BM 3.2) Miss 1 and Mister 2 start with \(u_1 = 1\), \(u_2 = -1\). Miss 1 plays A (multiply both by \(3\)) or B (multiply both by \(2\), then add \(5\) to \(u_2\)). Mister 2 observes and either Drops (D, game ends) or Continues (C), after which Miss 1 plays A or B once more. Draw the tree and count the pure strategies.


Solution. After A: \((3, -3)\); after B: \((2, 3)\). Continuing from \((3, -3)\) leads to \((9, -9)\) by A or \((6, -1)\) by B; continuing from \((2, 3)\) leads to \((6, 9)\) by A or \((4, 11)\) by B. Miss 1 moves at three nodes (the root and the two continuation nodes): \(2^3 = 8\) strategies. Mister 2 moves at two: \(2^2 = 4\) strategies. In reduced normal form, Miss 1’s plans at the continuation node after the move she did not make can be merged, leaving \(2 \times 2 = 4\) classes.


(BM 3.4) Javier and Krista buy a house. In September J buys Atlas (\(A\): J \(10\), K \(5\)) or waits (\(X\)). In October K buys Bellevue (\(B\): \(15\), \(28\)) or Cicada (\(C\): \(5\), \(12\)), or waits (\(X\)). In November J must buy Daffodil (\(D\): \(18\), \(15\)), Ember (\(E\): \(8\), \(35\)) or Floral (\(F\): \(40\), \(10\)). Write the normal form and find all pure NE.


Solution. J has \(2 \times 3 = 6\) strategies (AD, AE, AF, XD, XE, XF) and K has \(3\) (B, C, X). Rows AD, AE, AF give \((10, 5)\) in every column. Against B, C, X: XD gives \((15, 28)\), \((5, 12)\), \((18, 15)\); XE gives \((15, 28)\), \((5, 12)\), \((8, 35)\); XF gives \((15, 28)\), \((5, 12)\), \((40, 10)\). The pure NE are \((AD, C)\), \((AE, C)\), \((AF, C)\), \((XD, B)\) and \((XF, B)\). In the first three Krista’s choice of \(C\) is a (non-credible) threat that makes waiting unattractive to J.


(BM 4.6) The Count chooses Sword or Pistol; then the Duke chooses First blood or Last blood. With swords the Count wins with \(0.4\). With pistols the Count wins with \(0.7\), the Duke with \(0.2\), and both are shot with \(0.1\). At first blood the loser survives dishonoured (\(-20\)); at last blood the loser dies (\(-100\)); being shot is \(-100\); winning is \(+10\). Compute the expected payoffs, the normal form and the NE.


Solution. Expected payoffs (Count, Duke): \(SF\) \((-8, -2)\), \(SL\) \((-56, -34)\), \(PF\) \((-7, -22)\), \(PL\) \((-23, -78)\). For instance, \(PF\) gives the Duke \(0.2\cdot10 + 0.7(-20) + 0.1(-100) = -22\). (The printed solution has slightly different Duke payoffs; the conclusions are the same.) The Duke’s strategies say what to answer to S and to P: FF, FL, LF, LL. The pure NE are \((S, FL)\), \((P, FF)\) and \((P, LF)\). \((S, FL)\) rests on the Duke threatening last blood if pistols are chosen.


(BM 4.7) David picks a cake A, B or C; Emily, seeing it, shops at the Farmer’s market (F) or Grocery (G). The cake succeeds with probability \(p_{AF} = 0.5\), \(p_{AG} = 0.2\), \(p_{BF} = 0.8\), \(p_{BG} = 0.4\), \(p_{CF} = 0.7\), \(p_{CG} = 0.9\). Emily gets \(1\) for a success; David gets \(3\), \(2\), \(1\) times that for A, B, C. Write the “flat” simultaneous version and the true sequential normal form, and compare.


Solution. Flat: \((A, F) = (1.5, 0.5)\), \((A, G) = (0.6, 0.2)\), \((B, F) = (1.6, 0.8)\), \((B, G) = (0.8, 0.4)\), \((C, F) = (0.7, 0.7)\), \((C, G) = (0.9, 0.9)\). \(A\) is strictly dominated by \(B\); the flat game has NE \((B, F)\) and \((C, G)\). Sequentially, Emily’s strategies are pairs (answer to B, answer to C), ignoring A: the NE are \((B, FF)\), \((B, FG)\) and \((C, GG)\). The extra NE of the sequential form are again sustained by off-path plans.

From the course material:

Two players start with two peas each and alternate, A first. A move transfers to the opponent a positive number of peas never transferred before by anyone. A player who cannot move loses. Draw the tree and determine the winner.


Solution. Write states as (peas of A, peas of B; amounts used). A can open with 1 or 2.

A gives 2 → \((0, 4; \{2\})\). B replies by giving 1 → \((1, 3; \{1,2\})\): A’s only amount is 1, already used, so A loses.
A gives 1 → \((1, 3; \{1\})\). B replies by giving 2 → \((3, 1; \{1,2\})\): A’s only new feasible amount is 3 → \((0, 4; \{1,2,3\})\); B gives 4 → \((4, 0; \{1,2,3,4\})\), and A cannot give a new amount ≤ 4, so A loses. (B must avoid giving 3 instead, which would let A win by giving 2.)

Every opening loses against correct play: B wins. This is backward induction on a game of perfect information (Chapter 9).


In the sequential Battle of the Sexes, write Brian’s behavioural strategy equivalent to the mixed strategy \(p_{rr} = 0.1\), \(p_{rs} = 0.5\), \(p_{sr} = 0.2\), \(p_{ss} = 0.2\).


Solution. \(\sigma_B(r \mid x_1) = p_{rr} + p_{rs} = 0.6\) and \(\sigma_B(r \mid x_2) = p_{rr} + p_{sr} = 0.3\). (Many mixed strategies map to the same behavioural strategy: only these two marginals matter for outcomes.)

title: 9  Credibility and subgame perfection
text:
9.1 Nash equilibria of dynamic games
Nash equilibrium can be applied to dynamic games through their normal form, but it misses something essential: it treats a strategy as a commitment made before the game starts, so it accepts threats that the threatening player would never carry out when the moment comes. This chapter identifies the problem, solves perfect-information games by backward induction, and introduces Selten’s refinement — subgame-perfect equilibrium — which rules out non-credible threats. Stackelberg leader–follower games close the chapter.
The normal form of the sequential Battle of the Sexes (Chapter 8) has three pure Nash equilibria:
These strategies are chosen as if Brian moved first. \((R, rr)\) and \((R, rs)\) produce the same outcome: they coincide on the equilibrium path but differ off it. Out of equilibrium, \(rs\) is smarter; \(rr\) prescribes the irrational reply \(r\) to \(S\) — which never comes into play.
Why specify behaviour off the path at all? Because equilibria are sustained by beliefs about what others would do both on and off the path. \((S, ss)\) is a NE because Ann’s deviation to \(R\) is “punished”: Brian threatens to go to S anyway. But is the threat credible? Once Ann is at the romance movie, Brian’s best reply is \(r\).

title: 9  Credibility and subgame perfection
text:
9.2 Backward induction
In a dynamic game of perfect information every information set is a singleton. Take two players: player 1 chooses \(a_1 \in A_1\); player 2 observes \(a_1\) and chooses \(a_2 \in A_2(a_1)\); payoffs are \(u_1(a_1, a_2)\), \(u_2(a_1, a_2)\). When it is their turn, player 2 knows exactly where they are and solves \[R_2(a_1) = \arg\max_{a_2 \in A_2(a_1)} u_2(a_1, a_2).\] Thanks to complete information, player 1 anticipates this reaction and solves \(\max_{a_1} u_1(a_1, R_2(a_1))\). The resulting outcome \((a_1^*, R_2(a_1^*))\) is a Nash equilibrium in pure strategies.

Every finite game of perfect information has a backward-induction solution, which is a pure-strategy Nash equilibrium and is sequentially rational. If all terminal payoffs are different for each player, it is unique.

A consequence: every finite game of perfect information — tic-tac-toe, chess, go — has an optimal way to be played, and its value (win, draw, loss) is determined.

A chooses \(L\) (ending the game with payoffs \((2,0)\)) or \(R\). Then B chooses \(L'\) (payoffs \((1,1)\)) or \(R'\). Then A chooses \(L''\) (payoffs \((5,0)\)) or \(R''\) (payoffs \((3,2)\)).

Figure: the trust game; payoffs are (A, B).
At the last node A prefers \(L''\) (\(5 > 3\)). Anticipating this, B prefers \(L'\) (\(1 > 0\)). Anticipating that, A plays \(L\) (\(2 > 1\)). The outcome \((2,0)\) is Pareto dominated by \((3,2)\): rational players do not trust each other. A could promise to play \(R''\), but nothing makes the promise binding.

Imperfect information, two stages. If players 1 and 2 move simultaneously, then players 3 and 4 observe \((a_1, a_2)\) and move simultaneously, apply the same logic: for each \((a_1, a_2)\), let players 3 and 4 play a NE \((a_3^*(a_1, a_2), a_4^*(a_1, a_2))\) of the second-stage game; players 1 and 2 then play a NE of the first-stage game with payoffs \(u_j(a_1, a_2, a_3^*(\cdot), a_4^*(\cdot))\).

title: 9  Credibility and subgame perfection
text:
9.3 Subgame-perfect equilibrium

A (proper) subgame is a part of the tree that starts at a single node and contains all its successors, such that no information set is cut: if \(x\) belongs to the subgame and \(x' \in h_i(x)\), then \(x'\) belongs to the subgame too. The whole game is a subgame of itself.

A node inside a non-singleton information set cannot start a subgame — the player there does not know they are there.

A strategy profile is a subgame-perfect (Nash) equilibrium (SPE) if it induces a Nash equilibrium in every subgame.

An SPE is a NE that passes an additional test, so SPE is a refinement of NE. Every finite extensive-form game has an SPE (apply Nash’s theorem to the smallest subgames, replace them with their equilibrium payoffs, and proceed backwards). For finite games of perfect information, the SPE are exactly the backward-induction solutions.

If player 1 knows that action \(a_1\) triggers the response \(R_2(a_1)\), then a strategy of player 2 of the form “if \(a_1\) then \(a_2 \neq R_2(a_1)\)” is a non-credible threat. SPE eliminates them.


Brian’s strategy \(ss\) threatens to go to S even if Ann chooses R. In the subgame after \(R\), playing \(s\) is not a best response; so \((S, ss)\) is not an SPE. The unique SPE is \((R, rs)\). An extreme version: there is no sci-fi movie, \(S\) means “stay at home”, and after \(R\) Brian can comply (\(r\)) or harm himself (\(k\), payoffs \((-10, -99)\)). Threatening \(k\) might scare Ann into staying home, but carrying it out would be irrational: a non-credible threat.


Whatever the offer, accepting gives the responder something rather than nothing, so in every subgame R accepts. Anticipating this, P offers \(D\). Among the many NE, the unique SPE is “P offers \(D\); R accepts everything”. Refusing a low offer is a non-credible threat.







Experimental ultimatum games do not look like this: humans routinely refuse “insulting” offers. The SPE prediction is correct for the stated payoffs; the discrepancy says that real payoffs include fairness or spite, not that backward induction is wrong.

\((R, F)\) is the pure NE, with payoffs \((2, 2)\). Carl as leader: Joe’s best responses are \(F\) to \(R\) and to \(S\), \(G\) to \(T\); Carl’s payoffs are then \(2\), \(1\), \(4\), so he leads with \(T\): outcome \((T, G)\), payoffs \((4,3)\). Joe gets \(3\), above his minimax \(2\). Joe as leader: Carl’s best replies are \(R\) to \(F\), \(S\) to \(G\), and \(\{S, T\}\) to \(H\). Ties need a convention; with a generous follower (who breaks ties in the leader’s favour) and a generous leader (who breaks ties in the follower’s favour), Joe leads with \(H\) and Carl answers \(S\): outcome \((S, H)\), payoffs \((6, 4)\). Carl, the follower, gets \(6\), far above his minimax \(2\).


With ties broken in the leader’s favour, the leader’s Stackelberg payoff is at least their payoff in any pure Nash equilibrium of the static game (they could always lead with their NE strategy, to which the follower’s NE strategy is a best reply). The follower’s payoff is at least their minimax.

The follower is not necessarily worse off in general games. In zero-sum games, however, the leader’s gain is the follower’s loss — strange at first sight, since the follower has more information. In single-agent optimisation knowledge is power; in games ignorance can be bliss: the leader anticipates the follower’s informed reaction and restricts the follower’s useful options. This “first-mover advantage” returns in the Stackelberg duopoly of Chapter 11.

section: 9.5 Centipede games and the limits of backward induction
text:
9.5 Centipede games and the limits of backward induction
In a centipede game two players alternately choose to stop, taking the larger share of a growing pot, or continue, letting the pot grow and passing the move. Each stop is arranged so that the mover gains more by stopping now than by being stopped by the opponent at the next node. Backward induction then unravels from the last node: the last mover stops, so the one before stops, and so on. The unique SPE stops at the root, although continuing would make both far better off.
Experiments find that most subjects continue for several rounds. The prediction requires common knowledge of rationality at every node, including nodes that rationality says are never reached. A player who observes a continuation (an irrational move, by hypothesis) may reasonably doubt that the opponent will be rational later. Backward induction is most convincing in short games and for automated agents. Several exercises (house hunting, project hand-over, parties, joint projects) are centipede-like: whether the game unravels depends on whether stopping beats waiting at each node.

title: 9  Credibility and subgame perfection
section: 9.6 Commitment and the order of moves
text:
9.6 Commitment and the order of moves
Turning a simultaneous game into a sequential one changes what is credible.

The leader can always do at least as well as in some Nash equilibrium of the simultaneous game: by playing that equilibrium strategy, the follower’s best response reproduces it. Often the leader does strictly better (first-mover advantage, as in Stackelberg).
Moving first can also hurt: in Matching Pennies, being observed is fatal. Information about the leader’s move is valuable to the follower whenever the game has a competitive flavour.
Commitment is the power to make a threat credible by removing your own options: burning bridges, contracts, reputations, automated policies. Schelling’s paradox: limiting your own choices can raise your payoff, because it changes the opponent’s best response.

In a game with ties at terminal nodes, backward induction needs a tie-breaking rule. The usual conventions are a generous follower, who breaks ties in the leader’s favour, and a generous leader. Without such a rule the SPE need not be unique.

text:
9.7 Exercises
Problems from Badia and Marchioro (BM), Chapters 3 and 4.

(BM 3.1, continued) Find all SPE of the student–professor game. Which NE involve non-credible threats?


Solution. Every answer \(S\) gives P a positive payoff (\(3\), \(9\), \(15 > 0\)), so in every subgame P accepts: P plays \(SSS\). Anticipating this, U compares \(17\), \(20\), \(14\) and chooses \(x = 1\). The unique SPE is \((1, SSS)\). The NE \((1, SSN)\), \((1, NSS)\), \((1, NSN)\) have the same outcome but irrational plans off the path. \((0, SNS)\), \((0, SNN)\) and \((2, NNS)\) change the outcome through the non-credible threat of rejecting project \(1\) (the “strict professor”).


(BM 3.2, continued) Solve the Miss 1 / Mister 2 game by backward induction and give the SPE strategies. Is \(((A, A, A), (D, D))\) a NE?


Solution. At both final nodes Miss 1 plays A (\(9 > 6\) and \(6 > 4\)). Mister 2 then compares: after A, \(D\) gives \(-3\) and \(C\) gives \(-9\), so he drops; after B, \(D\) gives \(3\) and \(C\) gives \(9\), so he continues. Miss 1 compares \(3\) (A) with \(6\) (B). SPE: Miss 1 \((B; A, A)\) (root, after-A node, after-B node), Mister 2 \((D, C)\), with outcome \((6, 9)\). \(((A, A, A), (D, D))\) is a NE (payoffs \((3, -3)\); Miss 1 switching to B gets \(2\) under D), but not an SPE: dropping after B is a non-credible threat.


(BM 3.3) Lou asks Karen to go shopping on day 1. If she says No, Lou either Gives up or Requests again on day 2, and likewise on day 3, after which the game ends. Shopping on day \(d\) gives Karen \(d\) and Lou \(5 - 2d\); not shopping gives \(0\). Find the SPE and a NE that is not subgame perfect.


Solution. Day 3: Karen says Yes (\(3 > 0\)), giving Lou \(-1\). Day 2: Lou Gives up (\(0 > -1\)). Karen on day 2 says Yes (\(2 > 0\)). Day 1: Karen compares Yes (\(1\)) with No, after which Lou Requests (\(1 > 0\)) and she gets \(2\): she says No. The SPE is Karen \((N, Y, Y)\), Lou \((R, G)\), outcome day 2 with \((2, 1)\). Non-SPE NE: Lou \((G, G)\) and Karen \((Y, \cdot, \cdot)\). The threat of giving up immediately makes Karen accept on day 1, but Lou would not carry it out.


(BM 3.4, continued) Find the SPE of the house-buying game.


Solution. November: J buys F (\(40\)). October: K compares B (\(28\)), C (\(12\)), and waiting (\(10\), since J then buys F): she buys B. September: J compares A (\(10\)) with waiting (\(15\)). SPE \((XF, B)\), outcome Bellevue, \((15, 28)\). \((XD, B)\) has the same outcome but J’s plan to buy D in November is not optimal: it is a NE, not an SPE.


(BM 3.5) Yvonne (with a car) and Zoe (by bus) choose Beach or Disco simultaneously. Yvonne gets \(4\) at the beach and \(1\) at the disco; Zoe \(1\) and \(7\); each gets \(+5\) if together. If they are apart, Yvonne alone may Change location (costing her \(3\)) or Stay. Find the SPE outcome and Yvonne’s strategy.


Solution. After \((B, D)\): Change gives Yvonne \(1 + 5 - 3 = 3\), Stay gives \(4\), so she stays, \((4, 7)\). After \((D, B)\): Change gives \(4 + 5 - 3 = 6\), Stay gives \(1\), so she changes, \((6, 6)\). The reduced simultaneous game is \((B, B) = (9, 6)\), \((B, D) = (4, 7)\), \((D, B) = (6, 6)\), \((D, D) = (6, 12)\). \(D\) is dominant for Zoe, and Yvonne’s best response is \(D\). Outcome \((D, D)\) with \((6, 12)\); Yvonne’s SPE strategy is \((D;\ S \text{ after } (B, D),\ C \text{ after } (D, B))\). Yvonne’s flexibility hurts her: because she can always fix a mismatch, Zoe never needs to compromise.


(BM 3.6) Wife (7am and 7pm) and Husband (2pm) can each, at their turn, fix Food (benefit \(30\) to both, cost \(10\) to the doer), Clean (benefit \(50\), cost \(20\)) or do Nothing (\(+10\) to themselves). A chore cannot be repeated. The Wife’s 7am chores have \(10\%\) larger cost and benefit. Find the SPE.


Solution. Backward induction over the three-level tree gives the path: Wife does Nothing at 7am, Husband fixes Food, Wife Cleans at 7pm, with payoffs \((10 + 30 + 50 - 20,\ 30 + 50 - 10) = (70, 70)\). At 7pm the Wife does whichever chore remains if its benefit net of cost beats \(10\) (clean: \(30 > 10\); food: \(20 > 10\)). Anticipating this, the Husband prefers food to cleaning, and the Wife prefers to wait rather than pay the premium at 7am. The full SPE also specifies the Husband’s and the Wife’s moves in the 8 unreached subgames.


(BM 3.7) Anita and Ben simultaneously rush to the closet (5 candies) or the dining room (10 candies). In different rooms each keeps their candies; in the same room Anita proposes a split, giving Ben at least one candy, and Ben accepts or cries (both get \(0\)). Reduce the game by backward induction and find the SPE and a non-subgame-perfect NE.


Solution. In each ultimatum subgame Ben accepts anything positive, so Anita offers \(1\): \((4, 1)\) in the closet and \((9, 1)\) in the dining room. Reduced game: \((C, C) = (4, 1)\), \((C, D) = (5, 10)\), \((D, C) = (10, 5)\), \((D, D) = (9, 1)\). \(D\) is dominant for Anita and Ben answers \(C\). SPE: Anita plays \(D\) and offers \(1\) in either room; Ben plays \(C\) and accepts every offer. Non-SPE NE: Anita plays \(C\), Ben plays \(D\) and, in either bargaining subgame, accepts only splits leaving Anita a single candy. Outcome \((C, D)\) with \((5, 10)\). Anita does not deviate to \(D\), since she would then get at most \(1\). It is a NE because the threat is never tested, but crying when offered a positive amount is not credible.


(BM 3.8) Jeremy (odd days) and Kayla (even days) work on a project worth \(2^t\) on day \(t\). At the end of each day the worker Submits, getting \(2^t\) (the other gets \(60\%\)), or Hands over. After day \(10\) the project is worth \(0\). Find the SPE and a non-subgame-perfect NE.


Solution. On day \(10\) Kayla submits (\(1024 > 0\)). On day \(9\) Jeremy compares \(512\) (submit) with \(0.6 \times 1024 = 614.4\): he hands over. Inductively, at every \(t < 10\) handing over gives \(0.6 \cdot 2^{t+1} = 1.2\cdot2^t > 2^t\). SPE: always hand over before day \(10\); Kayla submits on day \(10\). Payoffs: Kayla \(1024\), Jeremy \(614.4\). This centipede does not unravel, because the pot grows fast enough. A non-SPE NE: Jeremy submits on day \(9\), and Kayla’s plan is to hand over even on day \(10\) (letting the deadline expire). Jeremy then rationally stops at \(9\); Kayla’s irrational plan is never tested.


(BM 3.9) In weeks \(0, 1, \dots, 5\) the Sorority (even weeks) and Fraternity (odd weeks) alternately decide to throw a Party or stop (N). A party costs the organiser \(10\) and gives both sections fun \(25\cdot0.6^j\) in week \(j\). Find the SPE. What if there is no deadline?


Solution. Cumulative payoffs (S, F) if the game stops after \(k\) parties: \(k = 0\): \((0, 0)\); \(1\): \((15, 25)\); \(2\): \((30, 30)\); \(3\): \((29, 39)\); \(4\): \((34.4, 34.4)\); \(5\): \((27.64, 37.64)\); \(6\): \((29.58, 29.58)\). Week 5: F stops (\(37.64 > 29.58\)). Week 4: S stops (\(34.4 > 27.64\)). Week 3: F stops (\(39 > 34.4\)). Week 2: S stops (\(30 > 29\)). Week 1: F parties (\(30 > 25\)). Week 0: S parties (\(30 > 0\)). SPE: S plays (P, N, N) and F plays (P, N, N) at their three nodes. Two parties are thrown, S stops in week 2, and the payoffs are \((30, 30)\). (The printed solution misreads its table and ends in week 4.) Without a deadline the same stationary profile, stopping from week 2 on, remains an SPE. From week 2 the organiser’s fun \(25\cdot0.6^j \leq 9\) is below the cost \(10\), so if the other will stop next, organising never pays (one-shot deviation principle).


(BM 3.11) Pirates of ranks \(1, \dots, n\): pirate 1 may take a pearl; whenever pirate \(k\) holds it, pirate \(k+1\) may kill him and take it. Each prefers (alive with pearl) \(\succ\) (alive without) \(\succ\) (dead). Solve for \(n = 5\) and \(n = 8\).


Solution. The captain \(n\) always takes the pearl (no one above him). So pirate \(n - 1\) never takes it (he would be killed), so pirate \(n - 2\) can take it safely, and so on: pirate \(j\) takes the pearl iff \(n - j\) is even. For \(n = 5\) (odd), pirate 1 takes the pearl and pirate 2 looks away. For \(n = 8\) (even), pirate 1 leaves the pearl. The SPE specifies the rule for every pirate, though only one or two ever move. The parity argument is typical of backward induction in long games.


(BM 4.6, continued) Which NE of the duel game are subgame perfect?


Solution. After S the Duke prefers F (\(-2 > -34\)); after P he prefers F (\(-22 > -78\)). So the Duke plays FF, and the Count compares \(-8\) (S) with \(-7\) (P). The unique SPE is \((P, FF)\). \((S, FL)\) relies on the threat of a duel to the death with pistols, which the Duke would not carry out. \((P, LF)\) has the right outcome but an irrational plan after S.


(BM 4.7, continued) Which NE of the cake game are subgame perfect?


Solution. Emily answers each cake with the shop that maximises its success probability: F after A and after B, G after C. David then compares \(1.5\) (A), \(1.6\) (B), \(0.9\) (C). The SPE is David B and Emily (F, F, G), outcome \((1.6, 0.8)\). Of the sequential NE \((B, FF)\), \((B, FG)\), \((C, GG)\) (strategies for B and C), only \((B, FG)\) is subgame perfect.

From the course material:

In the entry game, an entrant chooses Out (payoffs \((0, 2)\)) or Enter; after entry the incumbent chooses Accept (\((1,1)\)) or Fight (\((-1,-1)\)). Find all pure NE and the SPE.


Solution. Normal form: \((\text{Out}, \text{Fight})\) gives \((0, 2)\) and is a NE (entering against Fight gives \(-1\); the incumbent is indifferent since its move is off-path). \((\text{Enter}, \text{Accept})\) is a NE with \((1,1)\). Backward induction: after entry Accept beats Fight (\(1 > -1\)), so the entrant enters. The unique SPE is \((\text{Enter}, \text{Accept})\); \((\text{Out}, \text{Fight})\) rests on a non-credible threat.


Two investors each put 5000 € in a fund that pays \(x\) € each after 4 years if untouched. At the end of years \(1, 2, 3\) each may independently withdraw, getting \(6000 + 500t\) € for themselves (the other gets nothing); simultaneous withdrawal splits that amount; any withdrawal ends the game. Find the SPE for \(x = 7200\) and \(x = 8000\).


Solution. Solve backwards. Year 3: withdrawing gives \(7500\) (alone) or \(3750\) (both); keeping gives \(x\) if the other keeps, \(0\) if the other withdraws. For \(x = 7200\), Withdraw strictly dominates (\(7500 > 7200\), \(3750 > 0\)): both withdraw, \(3750\) each. For \(x = 8000\) the year-3 stage is a coordination game with NE (Keep, Keep) → \(8000\) and (Withdraw, Withdraw) → \(3750\). Year 2: withdrawing alone gives \(7000\). With continuation value \(3750\) (case \(x = 7200\), or \(x = 8000\) with the bad year-3 NE) Withdraw dominates; with continuation \(8000\), Keep–Keep is a NE (and so is Withdraw–Withdraw at \(3500\)). Year 1 repeats the logic with \(6500\). Hence for \(x = 7200\) the unique SPE has both withdrawing at year 1 (\(3250\) each), while for \(x = 8000\) there are SPE where both keep until the end (payoff \(8000\)) as well as SPE where both withdraw at the first opportunity.

title: 10  Multistage and repeated games
text:
10.1 Why exponential discounting
Many interactions consist of several rounds, each producing a partial payoff: tournaments, rounds of cards, partial exams, network sessions. This chapter studies multistage games (a sequence of static games played by the same players) and their most important special case, repeated games (the same stage game over and over). The central message is that the future can discipline the present: threats of punishment and promises of reward make cooperative behaviour — impossible in a one-shot Prisoner’s Dilemma — part of a subgame-perfect equilibrium.
Aggregating payoffs across periods requires a discounting rule. A single-person example shows why it must be exponential.
A player has a budget \(K = 1\) to spend over three periods with per-period utility \(u(x) = \log(1+x)\) and total value \(v = u(x_1) + \delta u(x_2) + \delta^2 u(x_3)\). The first-order conditions \(\frac{1}{1+x_1} = \frac{\delta}{1+x_2} = \frac{\delta^2}{1+x_3}\) give \[x_1 = \frac{3 - \delta - \delta^2}{1 + \delta + \delta^2}, \quad x_2 = \frac{-1 + 3\delta - \delta^2}{1 + \delta + \delta^2}, \quad x_3 = \frac{-1 - \delta + 3\delta^2}{1 + \delta + \delta^2},\] an equal split for \(\delta = 1\) and \((0.6393, 0.3115, 0.0492)\) for \(\delta = 0.8\) (an interior solution requires \(3\delta^2 - \delta - 1 \geq 0\), i.e. \(\delta \gtrsim 0.77\)). At period 2, with \(1 - x_1\) left, the player re-optimises \(u(x_2) + \delta u(x_3)\) and finds \(x_2 = (2 - x_1 - \delta)/(1 + \delta)\): for \(x_1 = 0.6393\) this is again \(0.3115\). Exponential discounting is time consistent — the plan made today is still optimal tomorrow.
Now try quasi-hyperbolic discounting, \(v = u(x_1) + \delta u(x_2) + \delta u(x_3)\) (the future discounted by a single factor). The plan is \(x_1 = (3 - 2\delta)/(1 + 2\delta)\), \(x_2 = x_3 = (2\delta - 1)/(1 + 2\delta)\), i.e. \((0.5385, 0.2308, 0.2308)\) for \(\delta = 0.8\). But at period 2 the player re-optimises with \(u(x_2) + \delta u(x_3)\) and chooses \((0.3675, 0.0940)\): the plan is inconsistent. A fully rational player anticipates this struggle between the present self and the future self; solving it by backward induction leads to \(x_1 = 1\) — overconsumption to prevent future misuse. From now on, discounting is always exponential.

10.2 Multistage games

A multistage game is a finite sequence of \(T\) normal-form stage games \(G_1, \dots, G_T\), played by the same players, with the outcome of each stage observed before the next. Stage payoffs \(u_i^{(t)}\) are aggregated with a common, commonly known discount factor: \[u_i = \sum_{t=1}^T \delta^{t-1} u_i^{(t)}.\]

Each stage is a simultaneous-move game, so the whole is a dynamic game of complete but imperfect information. A strategy specifies the first-stage action and the action at each later stage as a function of the history of outcomes.

If \(s^{t*}\) is a NE of stage game \(G_t\) for each \(t\), then playing \(s^{1*}, \dots, s^{T*}\) regardless of history is an SPE.
In any NE (even non-subgame-perfect) of a multistage game, a NE of \(G_T\) is played in the last stage.

holds because at the last stage there is no future to influence, so players simply best-respond. Statement (1) removes any strategic link between stages: in Prisoner–Revenge, “\(F\) then \(L\) whatever happened” and “\(F\) then \(G\) whatever happened” are SPE. But if the last stage has multiple equilibria, non-equilibrium play can be sustained earlier.


In Prisoner–Revenge, let both players use “play \(M\) in stage 1; then play Loner if the first outcome was \((M, m)\), otherwise Gang”. This is an SPE iff \(\delta \geq \tfrac13\).

Proof. A NE is played in every second-stage subgame, so it suffices to check the first stage. Against this strategy, \(M\) yields \(4 + 0\cdot\delta\) and \(F\) yields \(5 - 3\delta\); \(M\) is a best response iff \(\delta \geq \tfrac13\). \(\square\)
The construction is carrot and stick: play the desired (non-equilibrium) action now; reward compliance with the good equilibrium (carrot); punish deviation with the bad one (stick). \(\delta\) must be large enough for the difference to matter — for \(\delta = 0\) the stick is not a credible deterrent. The same trick can support any first-stage profile: \((F, m)\) is sustainable if Bob prefers \(-1 + 0\cdot\delta\) to \(1 - 3\delta\), i.e. \(\delta \geq \tfrac23\).

A strategy is optimal if no alternative strategy improves the payoff at any information set; it is one-stage unimprovable if no change of the action at a single information set does. In finite multistage games (and in infinite ones with discounting), a one-stage unimprovable strategy is optimal.

Proof idea. Suppose \(s_i\) is one-stage unimprovable but some \(s_i'\) does better. Take the profitable deviation with the fewest differences and consider its last deviation: in the subgame starting there, \(s_i'\) differs from \(s_i\) at a single information set and improves the payoff — contradiction. \(\square\)
To verify an SPE, it is enough to check one-shot deviations — exactly what backward induction does.

10.3 Finitely repeated games

\(G(T, \delta)\) is the multistage game in which the same stage game \(G\) is played \(T\) times, with discount \(\delta\). For \(T = \infty\) we need \(\delta < 1\); \(\delta\) may also be read as the probability that the game continues one more round.


If \(G\) has a unique NE \(s^*\), then \(G(T, \delta)\) with \(T < \infty\) has a unique SPE: play \(s^*\) at every stage.

In the twice-repeated Prisoner’s Dilemma (with \(4, 0, 5, 1\) and \(\delta = 1\)) the second stage always ends at \((F,F)\), so the first stage is a Prisoner’s Dilemma with every payoff raised by \(1\) — and \((F,F)\) is played twice. Repetitions of games with a unique equilibrium are uninteresting.

Now \((F,F)\) and \((H,H)\) are both NE. Consider “play \(M\); then \(H\) if the first outcome was \((M,M)\), otherwise \(F\)”. The first stage becomes the game with \((M,M)\) raised by \(3\) and everything else by \(1\), in which \((M,M)\), with payoffs \((7,7)\), is a NE (\(7 > 6\)). Cooperation is supported in the first stage even though \((M,M)\) is not an equilibrium of \(G\). Note that this needs no communication — only shared anticipation.

Remark (Punishing the punisher). Punishing with \((F,F)\) instead of \((H,H)\) hurts the punisher too, which invites renegotiation (“let’s forget it and play \((H,H)\)”). The construction is more robust with punishments that benefit the punisher: add strategies \(P\), \(Q\) with \((P,P)\) giving \((4, \tfrac12)\) and \((Q,Q)\) giving \((\tfrac12, 4)\). Then a deviation by Bob is punished by \((P,P)\) — good for Al — and vice versa. Cooperation is easier when punishments exist, and better still when several punishment options are available.

In finitely repeated games cooperation is therefore limited: the last stage is always played selfishly, and cooperative play requires multiple stage equilibria.

title: 10  Multistage and repeated games
text:
10.4 Infinitely repeated games
With \(T = \infty\) there is no last stage and backward induction cannot start. Surprisingly, this leads to a stronger conclusion: no external punishment equilibrium is needed.

In the Prisoner’s Dilemma, the grim-trigger strategy plays \(M\) at stage 1 and at every stage \(t > 1\) plays \(M\) if all previous outcomes were \((M,M)\); otherwise it plays \(F\) forever.


With stage payoffs \((M,M) = (4,4)\), \((M,F) = (0,5)\), \((F,F) = (1,1)\), both players using grim trigger is an SPE of \(G(\infty, \delta)\) iff \(\delta \geq \tfrac14\).

Proof. (NE) Suppose Al uses grim trigger. If Bob ever deviates, Al plays \(F\) forever, so Bob’s best continuation is \(F\) forever too. Deviating now yields \[V_{\text{dev}} = 5 + \delta + \delta^2 + \dots = 5 + \frac{\delta}{1 - \delta},\] while cooperating forever yields \(V_{\text{coop}} = 4/(1-\delta)\). \(V_{\text{coop}} \geq V_{\text{dev}}\) iff \(\delta \geq \tfrac14\). (SPE) Subgames come in two classes: after a history of \((M,M)\) only, the subgame is identical to the whole game, where grim trigger is a NE; after any deviation, grim trigger prescribes \((F,F)\) forever, which is a NE of that subgame. \(\square\)
The argument generalises.

A payoff vector is feasible if it is a convex combination of pure-strategy payoff vectors of \(G\) (achievable by alternating outcomes, or with a public randomisation device).


Let \(G\) be a finite static game of complete information, \((e_1, \dots, e_n)\) the payoffs of a NE of \(G\), and \((x_1, \dots, x_n)\) feasible payoffs with \(x_j > e_j\) for all \(j\). Then for \(\delta\) close enough to \(1\), \(G(\infty, \delta)\) has an SPE with average payoffs \((x_1, \dots, x_n)\).


Figure: feasible payoffs of the Prisoner’s Dilemma (the quadrilateral) and the payoffs above the NE \((1,1)\) that the folk theorem sustains (shaded).
Developments of the theorem:

Minimax punishment. In the Prisoner’s Dilemma the NE payoff coincides with the security payoff \(1\), but in general \(\text{maximin} \leq u(\text{NE})\), and harsher (still credible) punishments can push the threshold down to the minimax payoffs \((r_1, \dots, r_n)\).
Small \(\delta\). A lower discount factor weakens punishments; in some games (not the Prisoner’s Dilemma) punishments harsher than reverting to the NE are available — the Cournot carrot-and-stick of Chapter 11.

title: 10  Multistage and repeated games
text:
10.5 Tit for tat and reputation
Grim trigger holds a grudge forever. With two actions (cooperate / defect), tit for tat (TFT) plays at stage \(t\) whatever the opponent played at \(t-1\): it punishes immediately but forgives after one round (eye for an eye, live-and-let-live, reciprocal altruism in biology). TFT was the winner of Axelrod’s famous tournaments, but it is not subgame perfect: after a single unilateral deviation two TFT players alternate defection forever (a “death spiral”), which is not a NE of that subgame. Tit for two tats forgives the first defection and punishes the second; it avoids death spirals but is exploited by aggressive strategies.

In a one-shot trust game A either does Not trust (payoffs \((0,0)\)) or Trusts, after which B Collaborates \((1,1)\) or Defects \((-1,2)\). Backward induction predicts no trust. In the repeated game, A can use a grim trigger (“trust as long as B has always collaborated”), and B’s best response is to collaborate if \(\frac{1}{1-\delta} \geq 2\), i.e. \(\delta \geq \tfrac12\).
To strengthen B’s incentives, introduce a guarantor G who holds an insurance of \(2\) from B, keeps it if B defects, and otherwise returns it minus a fee of \(0.1\). With G, defecting no longer pays and trust is the SPE path. Why would G not simply keep the insurance? One-shot, keeping it is dominant. In the repeated game, G also has a reputation to protect: keeping the insurance yields \(2\) once, honest service yields \(0.1/(1-\delta)\), which is better iff \(\delta \geq 0.95\).

title: 10  Multistage and repeated games

10.6 Beyond Nash reversion
Friedman’s theorem punishes deviators by reverting to a stage NE forever. Two refinements widen and sharpen the picture.

Player \(i\)’s minmax (pure-strategy) payoff is \(\underline v_i = \min_{s_{-i}}\max_{s_i}u_i(s_i, s_{-i})\): the lowest payoff the others can hold \(i\) to, if \(i\) best-responds. A payoff vector is individually rational if \(x_i > \underline v_i\) for all \(i\).

No equilibrium of the repeated game can give a player less than \(\underline v_i\) on average: they could always best-respond at every stage. Conversely:

In an infinitely repeated game (satisfying a mild full-dimensionality condition), every feasible and individually rational payoff vector is the average payoff of some SPE, for all \(\delta\) close enough to \(1\).

The gain over Friedman lies between the minmax and the NE payoffs. Punishments harsher than the stage NE are possible, provided they are temporary and the punishers are themselves rewarded for carrying them out (“stick and carrot”, Abreu). With a stronger stick, a lower \(\delta\) suffices.
Checking an equilibrium. By the one-stage deviation principle, a profile is an SPE iff no player gains by deviating once, in any history, and then following the profile. Two kinds of history must be checked:

on the path: cooperating gives \(R/(1-\delta)\); the best one-shot deviation gives \(T\) now plus the discounted punishment phase;
off the path: the punishment itself must be a best response. Grim trigger passes, because it prescribes a stage NE. Tit for tat fails for some \(\delta\): after a single deviation it prescribes alternating \((C, D)\), \((D, C)\), …, and returning to cooperation may pay more. So tit for tat is a NE but generally not an SPE.

Alternating outcomes. Payoffs outside the pure-outcome set (a fair split of an asymmetric outcome) are reached by alternation. With \(\delta < 1\), the player who is favoured first gets slightly more: \((a + \delta b)/(1 - \delta^2)\) versus \((b + \delta a)/(1 - \delta^2)\).

10.7 Exercises
Problems from Badia and Marchioro (BM), Chapter 5. Several printed solutions contain slips; the corrected values are given here.

(BM 5.1) A guitarist and a pianist play two songs; for each song each Sings (S) or just Plays (J). \((S, S) = (5, 5)\); \((S, J) = (1, 6)\); \((J, S) = (7, 1)\); \((J, J) = (0, 0)\) (guitarist first). Payoffs add over the two songs. (a) Find the stage NE. (b) Find the SPE that repeats the same stage outcome and gives the highest total utility. (c) Is there an SPE in which the first song is a duet?


Solution. 

Pure NE \((S, J)\) and \((J, S)\), and a mixed one: the guitarist sings with \(1/2\), the pianist with \(1/3\), with payoffs \((7/3, 3)\). (b) Repeating \((J, S)\) gives \((14, 2)\), total \(16\); repeating \((S, J)\) gives \((2, 12)\), total \(14\). So \((J, S)\) twice. (c) No. A deviation from \((S, S)\) is detected and attributed: the guitarist deviating yields \((J, S)\), the pianist \((S, J)\). For the guitarist, \(5 + v_G(\text{reward}) \geq 7 + v_G(\text{punishment})\) needs a gap \(\geq 2\); the only stage NE giving him at least \(3\) is \((J, S)\). For the pianist the gap must be \(\geq 1\), so the reward must give him at least \(2\), which rules out \((J, S)\) (he gets \(1\)). No second-stage NE rewards both. (An exhaustive check over all assignments of the three stage NE confirms it. The printed solution overlooks the guitarist’s own incentive to deviate.)



(BM 5.2) At Christmas Ashley and Brook each give a gift (G, costing \(10\), worth \(100\) to the receiver) or not (N). At New Year’s Eve they choose Downtown or Home: \((D, D) = (50, 50)\), \((H, H) = (0, 0)\), mismatch \((-100, -100)\). The second stage is discounted by \(\delta\). Find a trivial SPE, and the smallest \(\delta\) for an SPE with gifts.


Solution. Stage 1 is a Prisoner’s Dilemma: \((G, G) = (90, 90)\), \((G, N) = (-10, 100)\), NE \((N, N)\). Stage 2 has NE \((D, D)\) and \((H, H)\). Trivial SPE: \((N, N)\) followed by either NE regardless of history. Carrot and stick: play \(G\); then \(D\) if both gave, \(H\) otherwise. Deviating gains \(100 - 90 = 10\) now and loses \(50\delta\) later, so the SPE requires \(\delta \geq 1/5\).


(BM 5.3) Ann and Brian play daily: both do chores \((-1, -1)\); only one does: the cleaner \(-2\), the other \(5\); neither \((0, 0)\); \(\delta = 0.9\). (a) Stage NE? (b) Show that “Ann always cleans” is not sustainable. (c) Show that alternating (Brian on odd days, Ann on even days) is, with a grim trigger.


Solution. 

\(N\) is dominant: NE \((N, N)\) with \((0, 0)\), which is also each player’s minmax. (b) Ann would average \(-2 < 0\): not individually rational, so no equilibrium can sustain it. (c) Grim trigger: follow the alternation; after any deviation play \(N\) forever. Values: Ann (lazy first) \(\frac{5 - 2\delta}{1 - \delta^2} = 16.8\), Brian \(\frac{-2 + 5\delta}{1 - \delta^2} = 13.2\). The binding check is whoever must clean today: cleaning gives \(\frac{-2 + 5\delta}{1 - \delta^2}\), deviating gives \(0\) forever, so the alternation is an SPE iff \(\delta \geq 0.4\). It holds at \(\delta = 0.9\). (The printed numerical values use \(1/(1-\delta^2) = 1.2345\) instead of \(5.263\); the conclusion is unaffected.)



(BM 5.4) Carl and Diana either Study or watch Movies in the library: \((S, S) = (10, 10)\), \((S, M) = (0, 18)\), \((M, S) = (15, 0)\), \((M, M) = (7.5, 9)\) (Carl first). (a) NE of \(G(3)\) with \(\delta = 1\)? (b) For which \(\delta\) does grim trigger sustain \((S, S)\) forever? (c) Add a punishment \(P\) giving \((-10, -10)\) whenever used. In \(G'(2)\), when can \((S, S)\) be played?


Solution. 

\((M, M)\) is the unique stage NE (dominant), so in \(G(3)\) it is played every night. (b) Diana: \(\frac{10}{1-\delta} \geq 18 + \frac{9\delta}{1-\delta}\), so \(\delta \geq 8/9\). Carl: \(10 \geq 15(1-\delta) + 7.5\delta\), so \(\delta \geq 2/3\). Grim trigger needs \(\delta \geq 8/9\). (c) \(G'\) has NE \((M, M)\) and \((P, P)\) (\(P\) is weakly dominated, but a NE). Play \((S, S)\) in round 1, then \((M, M)\) if round 1 was \((S, S)\) and \((P, P)\) otherwise. Diana: \(10 + 9\delta \geq 18 - 10\delta\), so \(\delta \geq 8/19\); Carl: \(10 + 7.5\delta \geq 15 - 10\delta\), so \(\delta \geq 2/7\). Hence \(\delta \geq 8/19\). Cooperation is possible only in round 1, since the last round must be a stage NE.



(BM 5.5) A warrior and a mage first choose Cast (C) or Draw (D): different actions give \(2\) each, equal actions \(0\), and \(1\) is subtracted from whoever uses their disliked action (C for the warrior, D for the mage). Then a troll appears: both Attack \((5, 5)\), a lone attacker dies (\(-100\)) while the other gets \(10\), both Run \((0, 0)\). Find all SPE.


Solution. Stage 1: \((C, C) = (-1, 0)\), \((C, D) = (1, 1)\), \((D, C) = (2, 2)\), \((D, D) = (0, -1)\). Stage 2 has a dominant action Run, with unique NE \((R, R)\). Since the last stage has a unique NE, nothing can be conditioned on stage 1. The SPE are: any stage-1 NE, then \((R, R)\) after every history. The stage-1 NE are \((C, D)\), \((D, C)\) and the mixed one, in which the warrior Casts with \(3/4\) and the mage Casts with \(1/4\) (each mixture makes the other indifferent; the printed \(1/2\) is a slip).


(BM 5.6) Two chipmunks search an Oak or a Pine: \((O, O) = (2, 2)\), \((O, P) = (3, 5)\), \((P, O) = (5, 3)\), \((P, P) = (1, 1)\). Then a wolf comes: both Help \((-1, -1)\), a lone helper is eaten (\(-100\)) while the other gets \(0\), both Flee \((-4, -4)\). Find all SPE.


Solution. Stage 2: Flee is dominant (\(0 > -1\), \(-4 > -100\)), so \((F, F)\) is the unique NE. Stage 1 NE: \((O, P)\), \((P, O)\), and both playing \(O\) with \(0.4\). SPE: one of these, then \((F, F)\) after every history. As in the previous problem, a unique last-stage NE leaves no room for rewards or punishments.


(BM 5.7) A knight and a thief simultaneously Attack the warlock or Save the princess. Both attack: \((0, 0)\); both save: \((-100, -100)\). Otherwise the hero who attacked may then Grab the wand and kill his ally (G) or be Fair (F). The knight values killing at \(-20\), the thief at \(20\) (the victim gets \(-100\)); a fair split gives \(10\) each. Reduce the game, find the SPE, and discuss \((AG, AG)\).


Solution. At the second move the knight plays \(F\) (\(10 > -20\)) and the thief plays \(G\) (\(20 > 10\)). Reduced game: \((A, A) = (0, 0)\), \((A, S) = (10, 10)\), \((S, A) = (-100, 20)\), \((S, S) = (-100, -100)\). \(A\) is dominant for the knight, and the thief answers \(S\). SPE \((AF, SG)\): the knight slays and is fair, the thief saves, and the thief’s betrayal plan is never used. \((AG, AG)\) is a NE: both attack, and the princess burns. Switching to \(S\) gives \(-100\) because of the other’s announced \(G\), and that threat is not credible for the knight.


(BM 5.8) In the infinitely repeated game \((M, M) = (1, 1)\), \((M, F) = (-2, 3)\), \((F, F) = (0, 0)\), describe tit for tat, find when it sustains \((M, M)\), and say whether it is an SPE.


Solution. Tit for tat: play \(M\) first, then copy the opponent’s previous move. Against tit for tat, defecting once and returning gives \(3 - 2\delta\) over two periods versus \(1 + \delta\); defecting forever gives \(3\) versus \(\frac{1}{1-\delta}\). Both require \(\delta \geq 2/3\). It is not an SPE in general: after a single deviation it locks the players into alternating \((M, F)\), \((F, M)\), The punisher’s echo is worth \(\frac{3 - 2\delta}{1-\delta^2}\), while forgiving restores \(\frac{1}{1-\delta} = \frac{1+\delta}{1-\delta^2}\). For \(\delta > 2/3\) forgiving is better, so tit for tat fails the one-shot deviation test off the path exactly when it works on the path (except at \(\delta = 2/3\)).


(BM 5.9) Stage game (rows/columns M, F, H): \((7,7)\) \((-2,9)\) \((-1,-1)\) / \((9,-2)\) \((2,2)\) \((0,0)\) / \((-1,-1)\) \((0,0)\) \((6,6)\), repeated twice. (a) Stage NE? (b) An SPE that plays \((M, M)\) first? (c) The condition on \(\delta\)?


Solution. 

\(M\) is strictly dominated by \(F\). Pure NE \((F, F)\) and \((H, H)\); mixed: each plays \(F\) with \(3/4\) and \(H\) with \(1/4\), with payoff \(1.5\) (the printed \(\tfrac14F + \tfrac34H\), payoff \(5\), inverts the weights). (b) Play \(M\); then \((H, H)\) if the first outcome was \((M, M)\), and \((F, F)\) otherwise. (c) Deviating to \(F\) gains \(2\) now and loses \(6 - 2 = 4\) later: \(9 + 2\delta \leq 7 + 6\delta\), so \(\delta \geq 1/2\).



(BM 5.10) Siblings play every afternoon: \((F, F) = (1, 1)\), \((B, F) = (3, -3)\), \((B, B) = (0, 0)\). Find strategies sustaining friendship forever. Do they work for \(\delta = 0.6\)?


Solution. Grim trigger: cooperating gives \(\frac{1}{1-\delta}\), the best deviation \(3 + 0\), so \(\delta \geq 2/3\). Tit for tat: a one-period deviation needs \(1 + \delta \geq 3 - 3\delta\) (\(\delta \geq 1/2\)), but permanent defection gives \(3\), so again \(\delta \geq 2/3\). At \(\delta = 0.6\) neither sustains cooperation (\(\frac{1}{0.4} = 2.5 < 3\)). The printed solution’s conclusion for \(\delta = 0.6\) is wrong. For \(\delta \geq 2/3\), grim trigger is an SPE; tit for tat is only a NE.

Solution. Pure NE of the stage game: \((F,F)\) and \((H,H)\) (check: against \(F\), \(F\) gives 2 > −2, 0; against \(H\), \(H\) gives 6 > −1, 0). Strategy: play \(M\); then \(H\) if the first outcome was \((M,M)\), else \(F\). Deviating from \(M\) to \(F\) in stage 1 yields \(9 + 2\delta\); complying yields \(7 + 6\delta\). The strategy is an SPE iff \(7 + 6\delta \geq 9 + 2\delta\), i.e. \(\delta \geq \tfrac12\); with \(\delta = 1\) it holds.


In the infinitely repeated Prisoner’s Dilemma with stage payoffs \((M,M) = (R,R)\), \((F,M) = (T, S)\), \((F,F) = (P,P)\) with \(T > R > P > S\), find the threshold on \(\delta\) for grim trigger to be an SPE.


Solution. Cooperating: \(R/(1-\delta)\). Deviating: \(T + \delta P/(1-\delta)\). Grim trigger is an SPE iff \(R \geq (1-\delta)T + \delta P\), i.e. \(\delta \geq \dfrac{T - R}{T - P}\). With \(T=5\), \(R=4\), \(P=1\) this gives \(\tfrac14\).

title: 11  Bargaining and dynamic duopolies
text:
11.1 Alternating-offer bargaining
Two important economic interactions unfold over time. In bargaining, players alternate offers to split a surplus that shrinks while they argue. In dynamic oligopoly, firms either move in sequence (Stackelberg) or compete repeatedly, which opens the door to tacit collusion. Both are solved with the tools of Chapters 9–10: backward induction, subgame perfection, and trigger strategies.
Two players must split a pie of size \(1\): player 1 gets \(x\), player 2 gets \(1 - x\). There are two approaches: the axiomatic Nash bargaining solution (Chapter 15) and the strategic model below (Ståhl, Rubinstein).
This is not a repeated game: an acceptance terminates it.
Deadline \(T = 1\) is the ultimatum game: many NE, but the unique SPE has the proposer keeping everything (\(x = 1\)) and the responder accepting.
Odd deadline \(T\). Player 1 makes the last offer; at stage \(T\) player 2 accepts anything, so player 1 takes the whole pie. At stage \(T-1\), player 2 knows that refusing gives player 1 \(\delta\) (in stage-\((T-1)\) units), so offers exactly \(x = \delta\), which is accepted. Iterating backwards, the SPE has immediate agreement with \[u_1 = \frac{1 + \delta^T}{1 + \delta}, \qquad u_2 = \frac{\delta - \delta^T}{1 + \delta}.\]
Delay is doubly costly: it shrinks the pie and merely leads to another, symmetric round of proposer–responder interaction, which rational players anticipate.
The limit \(T \to \infty\) of the finite formulas gives the same numbers, but uniqueness must be proved without backward induction. Proof sketch (Shaked–Sutton). Every subgame starting with a proposal is a copy of the whole game with the roles possibly swapped, so let \(M\) and \(m\) be the supremum and infimum of the proposer’s SPE payoff. A responder who refuses becomes the next proposer, worth between \(\delta m\) and \(\delta M\) today. Hence the responder accepts any offer above \(\delta M\), so the proposer gets at least \(1 - \delta M\): \(m \geq 1 - \delta M\). And the responder never accepts less than \(\delta m\), so \(M \leq 1 - \delta m\). Combining, \(M \leq 1 - \delta m \leq 1 - \delta(1 - \delta M)\), i.e. \(M(1 - \delta^2) \leq 1 - \delta\), so \(M \leq 1/(1+\delta)\); symmetrically \(m \geq 1/(1+\delta)\). Thus \(M = m = 1/(1+\delta)\). \(\square\)
The first-mover advantage \(1/(1+\delta) - \delta/(1+\delta) = (1 - \delta)/(1 + \delta)\) vanishes as \(\delta \to 1\): with patient players the split tends to \(50/50\).

At stage \(t = 1, 2, \dots\) a proposer offers a split and a responder accepts (the game ends) or refuses (the game moves to stage \(t+1\)). Player 1 proposes at odd stages, player 2 at even stages. If agreement on \((x, 1-x)\) is reached at stage \(t\), payoffs are \((\delta^{t-1} x, \delta^{t-1}(1-x))\) with \(0 < \delta < 1\): each round of delay wastes a fraction \(1 - \delta\) of the pie. If no agreement is reached by the deadline \(T\), both get \(0\).





In every SPE of the finite-horizon alternating-offer game, agreement is reached in the first round.



With an infinite horizon the alternating-offer game has a unique SPE: player 1 offers and player 2 immediately accepts \[u_1 = \frac{1}{1 + \delta}, \qquad u_2 = \frac{\delta}{1 + \delta}.\]

title: 11  Bargaining and dynamic duopolies
section: 11.2 Bargaining power: patience and proposal rights
text:
11.2 Bargaining power: patience and proposal rights
The Rubinstein argument generalises when players discount differently, with factors \(\delta_1, \delta_2\). Let \(x\) be what player 1 gets when proposing and \(y\) what player 2 gets when proposing. In the unique SPE each proposer offers the responder exactly the discounted value of becoming proposer next round: \[1 - x = \delta_2\,y, \qquad 1 - y = \delta_1\,x \quad\Longrightarrow\quad x = \frac{1 - \delta_2}{1 - \delta_1\delta_2}, \qquad 1 - x = \frac{\delta_2(1 - \delta_1)}{1 - \delta_1\delta_2}.\] Patience is power: as \(\delta_2 \to 1\) with \(\delta_1\) fixed, player 2 takes almost everything, even though player 1 proposes first. If both \(\delta_i = e^{-r_i\Delta}\) and the time between offers \(\Delta \to 0\), player 1’s share tends to \(\frac{r_2}{r_1 + r_2}\): the asymmetric Nash bargaining solution of Chapter 15 with weights inversely proportional to the impatience rates.
Legislative bargaining (Baron and Ferejohn, 1989). \(n\) legislators (odd) divide a budget by majority rule. Each round a randomly chosen member proposes a division; if a majority accepts, it is implemented; otherwise a new proposer is drawn and the budget is discounted by \(\delta\). In the stationary SPE the proposer buys the cheapest majority: offers \(\delta/n\) (the continuation value) to \((n-1)/2\) others, gives nothing to the rest, and keeps \[1 - \frac{n-1}{2}\cdot\frac{\delta}{n}.\] Agreement is immediate, the proposer captures much more than an equal share, and minimum winning coalitions form — features observed in real legislatures and committees.
Stationary strategies and wars of attrition. In infinite-horizon games whose subgames are scaled copies of the whole game (all Rubinstein-like problems), one looks for stationary equilibria: the action depends only on the current role (proposer or responder, mover or waiter), not on the date. The value of each role then solves a pair of equations like those above. When ending the game benefits the other player more than yourself, the game is a war of attrition: each wants the other to concede. Then there are typically two asymmetric pure equilibria (one side always concedes) and a mixed one in which each concedes with a constant probability per period, so delay is wasteful but possible.

title: 11  Bargaining and dynamic duopolies
text:
11.3 Stackelberg duopoly
Return to the Cournot setting (Chapter 4: price \(a - Q\), unit cost \(c\)), but now a leader (firm 1) chooses \(q_1\) first and a follower (firm 2) observes it before choosing \(q_2\).
By backward induction the follower plays its best response \[R_2(q_1) = \frac{a - q_1 - c}{2},\] and the leader maximises \(u_1(q_1, R_2(q_1)) = q_1\bigl(a - q_1 - R_2(q_1) - c\bigr) = q_1 (a - q_1 - c)/2\), giving \[q_1^* = \frac{a-c}{2}, \qquad q_2^* = \frac{a-c}{4}, \qquad u_1^* = \frac{(a-c)^2}{8}, \qquad u_2^* = \frac{(a-c)^2}{16}.\] Compared with Cournot (\(q = (a-c)/3\) each, profit \((a-c)^2/9\)), the leader produces more and earns more; the follower produces and earns less. Total output \(3(a-c)/4\) exceeds Cournot’s \(2(a-c)/3\).

Remark (Threats and information). The follower might threaten “choose the Cournot quantity or I will flood the market”. The threat is non-credible: flooding hurts the follower too. More interesting is the role of information. If the follower moved without observing \(q_1\), a chain of anticipations (“the leader will play \((a-c)/2\), so I play \((a-c)/4\), so the leader should play \(3(a-c)/8\), …”) leads back to Cournot. It is precisely the follower’s observation of \(q_1\) — common knowledge to both — that hands the leader the first-mover advantage. In multi-agent problems more information can make a player worse off.

title: 11  Bargaining and dynamic duopolies
section: 11.4 Collusion in a repeated Cournot duopoly
text:
11.4 Collusion in a repeated Cournot duopoly
At the Cournot equilibrium each firm earns \(u^C = (a-c)^2/9\), while sharing the monopoly output would give each \(u^m/2 = (a-c)^2/8\). The one-shot game cannot sustain this, but by the folk theorem an infinitely repeated one can.

Consider the strategy: produce \(q^m/2 = (a-c)/4\) at \(t = 1\) and as long as both firms have always done so; after any deviation produce the Cournot quantity \(q^C = (a-c)/3\) forever. Both firms using it is an SPE iff \(\delta \geq 9/17\).

Proof. After a deviation, \((q^C, q^C)\) forever is a NE of every subgame. On the cooperative path, the most profitable one-shot deviation against \(q^m/2\) is \(\arg\max_q q(a - q - (a-c)/4 - c) = 3(a-c)/8\), earning \(u^D = 9(a-c)^2/64\). Cooperation is optimal iff \[\frac{(a-c)^2/8}{1 - \delta} \geq \frac{9(a-c)^2}{64} + \frac{\delta}{1-\delta}\,\frac{(a-c)^2}{9} \iff \delta \geq \frac{9}{17}. \qquad \square\]
Less ambitious collusion. For \(\delta < 9/17\) the firms can still beat Cournot by targeting some \(q^* \in [q^m/2, q^C]\) with a grim trigger. Against \(q^*\), the best deviation \(q^D = (a - q^* - c)/2\) earns \(u^D = (a - q^* - c)^2/4\), while cooperation earns \(u^* = q^*(a - 2q^* - c)\) per period. The smallest sustainable \(q^*\) makes the incentive constraint \(u^*/(1-\delta) \geq u^D + \delta u^C/(1-\delta)\) binding: \[q^*(\delta) = \frac{(a - c)(9 - 5\delta)}{3(9 - \delta)},\] which moves continuously from \(q^C\) at \(\delta = 0\) to \(q^m/2\) at \(\delta = 9/17\).
Carrot and stick. Unlike the Prisoner’s Dilemma, the Cournot game offers punishments harsher than reverting to the NE. Abreu’s two-phase strategy uses a reward action \(R\) (produce \(q^m/2\)) and a punishment action \(P\) (produce some \(x > q^C\)):

start with \(R\);
play \(R\) if both played \(R\) in the previous period, or if both played \(P\);
otherwise play \(P\).

A deviator is punished for one period with low prices, and the punishment itself is enforced because deviating from it restarts it. One can check that with \(\delta = \tfrac12\) and \(x = 2(a-c)/5\) the strategy is an SPE: the monopoly split is sustained even though \(\tfrac12 < 9/17\).






Competition authorities fine firms that meet to fix prices or quantities. The repeated-game analysis shows why this is not enough: a grim-trigger agreement needs no meeting and no communication. It can be reached “in the CEO’s head”, as a mutually understood equilibrium of the repeated game — tacit collusion.

(BM 3.10) Amelie (odd days) and Bernard (even days) work on a project worth \(v_1\) on day 1 and \(v_{j+1} = \delta v_j\) afterwards. On their day, the mover either Calls the end (C), getting \(0.4v_j\) while the other gets \(0.6v_j\), or Keeps working (K). Show that in any stationary SPE the project ends by day 2, and find for which \(\delta\) Amelie ends it.


Solution. Every subgame starting on an odd (even) day is the day-1 game scaled by \(\delta^{j-1}\), with roles swapped on even days. So a stationary strategy depends only on whether one is the mover. If the mover’s rule were “keep” for both, payoffs would be \(0 < 0.4\), so somebody calls by day 2. Amelie compares \(0.4v_1\) (call now) with \(0.6\delta v_1\) (Bernard calls tomorrow). For \(\delta < 2/3\) calling is better for every mover, and the unique SPE is that Amelie ends the project on day 1. For \(\delta > 2/3\) being the non-caller is worth waiting for, and there are two pure stationary SPE: Amelie always keeps and Bernard always calls (the project ends on day 2), or Bernard always keeps and Amelie always calls (it ends on day 1). This is a war of attrition, in which each wants the other to concede. (The printed solution states the inequality the wrong way round.)

In the alternating-offer game with deadline \(T = 2\) (player 1 proposes first, player 2 proposes last), find the SPE.


Solution. At stage 2 player 2 proposes and keeps everything: payoffs \((0, \delta)\). At stage 1 player 1 offers player 2 exactly \(\delta\) and keeps \(1 - \delta\); player 2 accepts. Verify the carrot-and-stick strategy for \(a - c = 1\), \(\delta = \tfrac12\), \(x = \tfrac25\).


Solution. Reward profit \(\tfrac18\); punishment profit (both at \(0.4\), price \(0.2\)) is \(0.08\). Value on the reward path \(V_R = \tfrac18 / (1 - \tfrac12) = 0.25\). Value at the start of a punishment phase with compliance \(V_P = 0.08 + \tfrac12 V_R = 0.205\). Reward phase: best deviation \(q = \tfrac38\) earns \(\tfrac{9}{64} \approx 0.1406\), then punishment: \(0.1406 + \tfrac12 \cdot 0.205 = 0.243 < 0.25\). Punishment phase: best deviation against \(0.4\) is \(q = 0.3\), earning \(0.09\), then punishment restarts: \(0.09 + \tfrac12 \cdot 0.205 = 0.1925 < 0.205\). No profitable one-shot deviation exists, so by the one-stage deviation principle the strategy is an SPE.

title: 12  Bayesian games
text:
12.1 Types and the common prior
Until now every player knew everyone’s payoffs. In reality a firm does not know a competitor’s costs, a bidder does not know the others’ valuations, a network node does not know whether its neighbour is selfish or malicious. Harsanyi’s insight was that such incomplete information can be absorbed into the familiar framework: let Nature draw each player’s private characteristics — their type — from a commonly known distribution, and let players form beliefs about types just as they form beliefs about actions. This chapter defines static Bayesian games and Bayesian Nash equilibrium and works through the standard examples.
Harsanyi (1967–68) turned incomplete into imperfect information by adding a preliminary move of Nature:
The result is a dynamic game in which players do not observe all of Nature’s move. Types need not describe preferences only: they can capture what a player knows about the world or about other players.
To best-respond, the entrant needs beliefs about the incumbent’s type. We assume that players do not know the opponents’ types but know how they are drawn:

12.2 Type-contingent strategies
A strategy must now say what each type does. In the entry game the entrant has one type and two strategies; the incumbent moves at two information sets (one per type) and has four strategies \(xy\): \(x\) for the rational type, \(y\) for the crazy type. Expected payoffs follow from the prior; for instance under \((E, AF)\) the entrant gets \(p \cdot 1 + (1-p)(-1) = 2p - 1\) and the incumbent \(p \cdot 1 + (1-p) \cdot 2 = 2 - p\):
