Only \((E, AF)\) is sequentially rational: each incumbent type does what is best for that type once entry has occurred (a rational incumbent accepts, a crazy one fights). If \(p < \tfrac12\), then \(2p - 1 < 0\) and the sensible outcome becomes \((O, AF)\): the incumbent always plays \(AF\), and the entrant decides on the basis of the prior.

Remark (Type agents). The entrant averages over the incumbent’s types — natural. The incumbent, oddly, “takes expectations over its own types”: the real players (rational 2, crazy 2) are replaced by a single meta-player choosing a plan for both. This type-agent representation gives the right best responses because a plan maximises the expected payoff iff each type’s component maximises that type’s payoff (the types’ choices do not interact). The common prior is a strong assumption — it must hold for players to be able to conjecture the outcome — and its realism must be checked in every application.

title: 12  Bayesian games
text:
12.3 Static Bayesian games

A static Bayesian game is \[G = \{\mathcal N;\ A_1, \dots, A_n;\ T_1, \dots, T_n;\ \phi_1, \dots, \phi_n;\ u_1, \dots, u_n\},\] where \(A_i\) are action sets, \(T_i\) type spaces, \(\phi_i(t_{-i} \mid t_i)\) player \(i\)’s beliefs about the others’ types, and \(u_i(a_1, \dots, a_n; t_i)\) type-dependent payoffs.


Private values means \(u_i\) depends only on \(t_i\); with common (interdependent) values \(u_i\) depends on the whole type vector.
Types can also restrict actions: if action \(H\) is available only with probability \(q\), give player \(i\) two types and set all payoffs of \(H\) to \(-\infty\) for the second type.
With a common prior \(\phi(t_1, \dots, t_n)\), beliefs are posteriors by Bayes’ rule, \(\phi_i(t_{-i} \mid t_i) = \phi(t_i, t_{-i}) / \phi(t_i)\). Types are independent if \(\phi = \prod_i \phi(t_i)\), in which case beliefs equal the marginals.
In principle one should model beliefs about beliefs about beliefs…; Harsanyi showed that the common prior collapses this hierarchy to first-order beliefs.


A pure strategy of player \(i\) is a map \(s_i : T_i \to A_i\); a mixed strategy is a distribution over such maps.

Why specify what every type does, when only one type is real? Not for player \(i\) — but for the others, who need to form beliefs about \(i\)’s behaviour. (The same reason led us to specify off-path behaviour in dynamic games.) From the opponents’ viewpoint, a player using a type-dependent pure strategy with randomly drawn type is indistinguishable from one using a mixed strategy.

A profile \(s^* = (s_1^*, \dots, s_n^*)\) is a Bayesian Nash equilibrium (BNE) if for every player \(i\) and every type \(t_i \in T_i\), the action \(s_i^*(t_i)\) maximises \(i\)’s expected payoff given their beliefs: \[s_i^*(t_i) \in \arg\max_{a_i \in A_i} \sum_{t_{-i}} \phi_i(t_{-i} \mid t_i)\; u_i\bigl(a_i, s_{-i}^*(t_{-i}); t_i\bigr).\]

Equivalently, \(\mathbb E[u_i(s_i^*(t_i), s_{-i}^*(t_{-i}); t_i) \mid t_i] \geq \mathbb E[u_i(a_i, s_{-i}^*(t_{-i}); t_i) \mid t_i]\) for all \(a_i\): nobody wants to change given what they know, and what they don’t know they estimate. With continuous types the sums become integrals.

title: 12  Bayesian games
text:
12.4 Harsanyi’s purification of mixed strategies
Mixed strategies were interpreted as beliefs (Chapter 5). Harsanyi made this precise: a mixed equilibrium is the limit of pure equilibria of slightly perturbed games of incomplete information.
Perturb the Battle of the Sexes: Ann’s payoff at \((R,R)\) becomes \(2 + c\) and Brian’s at \((S,S)\) becomes \(2 + d\), where \(c, d\) are independent, uniform on \([0, x]\), and privately known. Look for threshold strategies: Ann plays R iff \(c > C\); Brian plays S iff \(d > D\).
Ann does not know \(d\); Brian plays R with probability \(D/x\). Her expected payoffs are \((2 + c) D/x\) from R and \(1 - D/x\) from S, so she plays R iff \(c \geq x/D - 3\); hence \(C = x/D - 3\). Symmetrically \(D = x/C - 3\). Thus \(C = D\) and \[C^2 + 3C - x = 0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad C = \frac{-3 + \sqrt{9 + 4x}}{2}.\] Ann plays R with probability \[1 - \frac{C}{x} = \frac{2x + 3 - \sqrt{9 + 4x}}{2x} \xrightarrow[x \to 0]{} \frac23,\] which is exactly her probability in the mixed NE. As the perturbation vanishes, players who never actually randomise generate, from each other’s viewpoint, the mixed equilibrium.

Check type by type: against \(DC\) the opponent drives with probability \(\tfrac12\); an L-type gets \(\tfrac12 \cdot 4 + \tfrac12 \cdot 8 = 6 > 0\) by driving, an H-type gets \(\tfrac12 (4 - 16) + \tfrac12 \cdot 8 = -2 < 0\).


A jury of two decides whether to Acquit or Convict; conviction requires both votes. The defendant is guilty (G) with common prior \(q > \tfrac12\). Each juror gets payoff \(1\) for a correct verdict, \(0\) otherwise. Without further information C is dominant.
Now each juror receives a private, conditionally independent signal \(t_i \in \{t_G, t_I\}\) with \(\Pr[t_G \mid G] = \Pr[t_I \mid I] = p > \tfrac12\) — a binary symmetric channel. A lone juror would update \[\Pr[G \mid t_G] = \frac{qp}{qp + (1-q)(1-p)} > q, \qquad \Pr[G \mid t_I] = \frac{q(1-p)}{q(1-p) + (1-q)p},\] and the latter is below \(\tfrac12\) iff \(p > q\): when the signal is more informative than the prior, a lone juror follows it.
With two jurors, is “follow the signal” (\(CA\): convict on \(t_G\), acquit on \(t_I\)) an equilibrium? The key is pivotality: a vote matters only if the other juror votes C, i.e. (under \(CA\)) only if the other received \(t_G\). Conditioning on that event, \[\Pr[G \mid t_1 = t_I, t_2 = t_G] = \frac{q\,p(1-p)}{q\,p(1-p) + (1-q)(1-p)p} = q > \tfrac12,\] so a juror with an innocent signal should convict: \(CA\) is not a best response to itself. Reasoning about the pivotal event biases jurors toward conviction, even against their own informative signal. (For \(p \leq q\), \((CC, CC)\) is a BNE; for \(p > q\) the symmetric equilibrium has \(t_I\)-jurors convicting with a probability strictly between \(0\) and \(1\), as in Feddersen and Pesendorfer’s analysis of the unanimity rule.)


Two students share a project. Each either puts Effort (cost \(c\)) or Shirks. The project succeeds if at least one puts effort, giving student \(i\) value \(t_i^2\), with \(t_i \sim \mathcal U[0,1]\) privately known:

title: 12  Bayesian games
text:
12.6 Two classic applications
Cournot with a private cost. Firm 1 has unit cost \(c\), known to all. Firm 2’s cost is \(c_H\) with probability \(\theta\) and \(c_L\) otherwise, known only to firm 2; demand is \(a - Q\). Each type of firm 2 best-responds to \(q_1\), and firm 1 best-responds to firm 2’s expected output: \[q_2(c_2) = \frac{a - c_2 - q_1}{2}, \qquad q_1 = \frac{a - c - \mathbb E[q_2]}{2} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad q_1^* = \frac{a - 2c + \bar c_2}{3},\qquad \bar c_2 = \theta c_H + (1-\theta)c_L,\] and \(q_2^*(c_2) = \frac{2a + 2c - 3c_2 - \bar c_2}{6}\). Compared with complete information, the high-cost type produces more (by \((c_H - \bar c_2)/6\)) and the low-cost type less. Firm 1 cannot tailor its output to the true cost, so each type of firm 2 faces an “average” rival.
Adverse selection: the market for lemons (Akerlof, 1970). Used cars have quality \(\theta \sim \mathcal U[0, 1]\), known to the seller, who values a car at \(\theta\); buyers value it at \(\tfrac32\theta\). Trade would be efficient for every car. At a price \(p\) only owners with \(\theta \leq p\) sell, so the average quality on offer is \(p/2\) and buyers are willing to pay \(\tfrac32\cdot\tfrac p2 = \tfrac34p < p\). No price clears the market, and only \(\theta = 0\) trades. Private information can destroy a market completely. Warranties, inspections, reputation and signalling (Chapter 13) exist to repair it.

Remark (A taxonomy of dynamic Bayesian games). When the uninformed player moves first and the informed one reacts (a screening or Bayesian entry game), the uninformed player can only use the prior. Backward induction on each type’s decision node gives a subgame-perfect answer, and no belief updating is needed. When the informed player moves first (a signaling game), the action may reveal the type, and the responder’s beliefs after each action must be specified. This is where perfect Bayesian equilibrium (Chapter 13) is required.

title: 12  Bayesian games
text:
12.7 Exercises
Problems from Badia and Marchioro (BM), Chapter 6: static Bayesian games and screening games.

(BM 6.1) Stevie is Good (G) or Naughty (N). If naughty, he gets nothing: Stevie \(0\), parents \(-10\). If good, the parents give a Sweater (\(-10\) for Stevie, \(0\) for them) or a Train (\(+40\) for Stevie, \(+20\) for them), but the train costs them \(50\) unless Santa exists. Stevie believes Santa exists with probability \(p\); the parents know. Write the type-agent normal form and find the pure BNE for \(p = 0.9\). Which are subgame perfect?


Solution. The parents’ strategies are pairs (Santa, no Santa). Row G: SS \((-10, 0)\), ST \((40 - 50p, 30p - 30)\), TS \((50p - 10, 20p)\), TT \((40, 50p - 30)\); row N: \((0, -10)\) throughout. For \(p = 0.9\): G gives \((-10, 0)\), \((-5, -3)\), \((35, 18)\), \((40, 15)\). BNE: \((N, SS)\), \((N, ST)\), \((G, TS)\). Only \((G, TS)\) is subgame perfect: giving a sweater when the train is free is not optimal. Stevie behaves because he believes in Santa: against TS, being good is worth \(50p - 10\), so for \(p < 0.2\) he would be naughty.


(BM 6.3) An opportunistic transmitter T either Buys a licensed channel (\(-10\); the incumbent S gets \(100\)) or Accesses S’s band. S then Combats it (T gets \(-20\); S gets \(90\) with high power, \(50\) without) or does nothing (T \(20\), S \(80\)). S has high power with probability \(p = 0.7\). Find the BNE and the SPE.


Solution. S’s strategies are (high, low). Row A: CC \((-20, 78)\), CD \((-8, 87)\), DC \((8, 71)\), DD \((20, 80)\); row B: \((-10, 100)\). BNE: \((A, CD)\) and \((B, CC)\). Sequential rationality requires C when strong (\(90 > 80\)) and D when weak (\(80 > 50\)), so CD. Then T compares \(-8\) (A) with \(-10\) (B) and accesses. SPE \((A, CD)\). In \((B, CC)\) the weak incumbent’s threat to fight is not credible. This is the Bayesian entry game in a cognitive-radio setting.


(BM 6.4) Henchmen Franco and Gino each act Conspicuously or Inconspicuously. At least one C gives a reward of \(10\) each, but both C gets them arrested (\(-30\)). With probability \(p = 0.3\) Franco is an undercover cop, who gets \(20\) if both are arrested and \(0\) otherwise. Find the BNE.


Solution. Franco’s strategies are (cop, crook). For \(p = 0.3\) the payoffs (Gino, Franco) are: Gino C against CC, CI, IC, II gives \((-30, -15)\), \((-2, 13)\), \((-18, -21)\), \((10, 7)\); Gino I gives \((10, 7)\), \((3, 0)\), \((7, 7)\), \((0, 0)\). Gino’s best responses are I, I, I, C. Franco’s best response to C is CI, and to I it is CC or IC. Pure BNE: \((CC, I)\) and \((IC, I)\). In general, Gino plays I, the crook plays C, and the cop is indifferent, so any mixture of the cop’s actions is part of a BNE. With a single information set for Gino, every BNE is subgame perfect. The PBE beliefs on Gino’s four nodes are \((0.3\alpha, 0.3(1-\alpha), 0.7, 0)\).


(BM 6.5) Short-sighted John Greets or Ignores a girl who is Camilla with probability \(p = 0.3\). Ignoring gives John \(-20\), and the girl \(-50\) if she is Camilla (\(0\) otherwise). After a greeting she Waves (John \(10\); the girl \(30\) if Camilla, \(10\) otherwise) or stays Silent (John \(-50\) and Camilla \(10\) if she is Camilla; \(0\) and \(0\) otherwise). Find the BNE.


Solution. Row G against SS, SW, WS, WW: \((-15, 3)\), \((-5, 10)\), \((3, 9)\), \((10, 23)\); row I: \((-20, -15)\) throughout. Waving is optimal for both types, and John’s best response to WW is G. Ignoring is never a best response (every G entry exceeds \(-20\)). The unique BNE \((G, WW)\) is also the SPE, and John’s belief is simply the prior.


(BM 6.11) Emma (Aquamarine or Beige) and Frank (Azure or Brown) dress for a wedding. Matching azure gives \(3\) each, matching brown \(2\), mismatch \(0\). With probability \(p = 0.8\) Frank’s suits are dirty: a dirty brown suit costs both \(1\); a dirty azure suit costs Frank \(3\) and Emma \(5\). Find the pure BNE.


Solution. Frank’s strategies are (dirty, clean). Emma A against AA, AB, BA, BB: \((-1, 0.6)\), \((-1.6, 0)\), \((-0.2, -0.2)\), \((-0.8, -0.8)\); Emma B: \((-4, -2.4)\), \((-3.6, -2)\), \((0.8, 0.8)\), \((1.2, 1.2)\). Against A, both of Frank’s types match with A (dirty: \(0 > -1\); clean: \(3 > 0\)), and against AA Emma prefers A (\(-1 > -4\)). Against B, both types play B, and Emma prefers B. Two pure BNE: \((A, AA)\) and \((B, BB)\), the second Pareto dominant. (The printed solution lists only \((B, BB)\).) Incomplete information has turned a coordination game into one where the matching colour is worse when dirty, but coordination on azure still survives.


(BM 6.13) Alberto and Gianluca apply to Coimbra or Santander. Gianluca gets \(2\) (together in C), \(1\) (together in S), \(0\) apart. With probability \(p\) Alberto is chasing a girl in Santander: then S is dominant, giving him \(2\) (C gives \(0\)). Otherwise he has Gianluca’s preferences. Find the pooling BNE, and the values of \(p\) for which a separating BNE exists.


Solution. Against Alberto’s pooling SS, Gianluca plays S (\(1 > 0\)), and S is a best response for both of Alberto’s types: \((SS, S)\) is a BNE for every \(p\). If Gianluca plays C, Alberto’s best response is SC (the chaser goes to S, the other to C). Against SC Gianluca gets \(2(1 - p)\) from C and \(p\) from S. So \((SC, C)\), a separating BNE, exists iff \(p \leq 2/3\). With a small chance of romance, the friends can still coordinate on the better destination.


(BM 6.14) Jane Keeps her €10 000 or buys a Car (€8000; worth €5000 after a year). Simultaneously the bank Leaves the money (5% interest) or buys Subprime bonds: a good bank (probability \(p = 0.2\)) earns 15%, a bad bank loses everything. The bank’s payoff is the interest \(G\) if positive, \(-G/5\) otherwise. Find the BNE.


Solution. In k€: for Jane, K–L gives \(10.5\), K–S gives \(11.5\) (good bank) or \(0\) (bad bank); C–L gives \(7.1\), C–S gives \(7.3\) or \(5\). The bank’s payoffs are \(0.5\), \(1.5\), \(2\) and \(0.1\), \(0.3\), \(0.4\) respectively. For both types of bank, S is strictly better whatever Jane does, so SS is dominant. Against SS, Jane gets \(11.5p = 2.3\) from K and \(5 + 2.3p = 5.46\) from C. The unique BNE is \((C, SS)\): Jane spends her money because the bank would gamble it away. The incentive structure (\(-G/5\) rewards losses) is what makes every type of bank reckless.


(BM 6.17) A thief Enters or Flees; simultaneously the sheriff Patrols or Quits. The sheriff is armed with probability \(0.3\). Flee: thief \(0\), and the sheriff \(-10\) if patrolling, \(0\) if quitting. Enter against Quit: thief \(10\), sheriff \(0\). Enter against Patrol: if armed, thief \(-100\) and sheriff \(20\); if unarmed, both \(-20\). Find the BNE.


Solution. Sheriff strategies are (armed, unarmed). Thief E against PP, PQ, QP, QQ: \((-44, -8)\), \((-23, 6)\), \((-11, -14)\), \((10, 0)\); F: \((0, -10)\), \((0, -3)\), \((0, -7)\), \((0, 0)\). An unarmed sheriff never patrols (\(-20\) or \(-10 < 0\)), so PP and QP are out, and there is no pure BNE (QQ invites entry, PQ deters it). The armed sheriff mixes P with \(\rho\), the thief enters with \(\varepsilon\). Armed indifference: \(20\varepsilon - 10(1 - \varepsilon) = 0\), so \(\varepsilon = 1/3\). Thief indifference: \(0.3(10 - 110\rho) + 0.7\cdot10 = 0\), so \(\rho = 10/33\). The unarmed sheriff stays home; the armed one patrols with probability \(10/33\).

From the course material:

Two interns independently choose an operating system, M or W. Each prefers M with probability \(p\) and W with probability \(1-p\) (independently, privately known, \(p\) common knowledge). Using the favourite OS gives \(1\), the other \(0\); choosing the same OS as the partner adds \(2\). For which \(p\) is “follow your type” a BNE?


Solution. Suppose the partner follows their type: they choose M with probability \(p\). An M-type gets \(1 + 2p\) from M and \(0 + 2(1-p)\) from W; M is optimal iff \(1 + 2p \geq 2 - 2p\), i.e. \(p \geq \tfrac14\). A W-type gets \(1 + 2(1-p)\) from W and \(2p\) from M; W is optimal iff \(3 - 2p \geq 2p\), i.e. \(p \leq \tfrac34\). “Follow your type” is a BNE iff \(\tfrac14 \leq p \leq \tfrac34\); outside this range the minority type conforms to the likely choice of the majority.


In the study-group game with \(c = 0.125\), compute the equilibrium probability that the project fails.


Solution. \(\theta^* = 0.125^{1/3} = 0.5\). Each student shirks with probability \(0.5\); the project fails iff both shirk: probability \(0.25\). (A single student working alone would shirk only if \(t < \sqrt{0.125} \approx 0.354\).)

title: 13  Perfect Bayesian equilibrium and signaling
text:
13.1 Why SPE is not enough
Static Bayesian games are solved by Bayesian Nash equilibrium; dynamic games of complete information by subgame-perfect equilibrium. When both features are present — a player with private information moves, and others react after observing the move — neither concept is enough: Nature’s initial move merges all subtrees into a single subgame, so subgame perfection loses its bite. This chapter introduces beliefs at every information set and the resulting perfect Bayesian equilibrium, then applies it to signaling games, reputation building, and cheap talk.
Entry with an uncertain entrant. Let the entrant now have two types: Competitive (probability \(p = \tfrac12\)), with the payoffs of Chapter 12 (entry is met by Accept \((1,1)\) or Fight \((-1,-1)\)), or Weak, for whom entering is always bad: Accept gives \((-1, 1)\), Fight \((-2, 0)\). Staying out gives \((0,2)\) to either type. The incumbent observes entry but not the type, so it cannot apply backward induction. The entrant’s strategies are \(OO, OE, EO, EE\) (action of C, action of W):
There are two pure NE: \((EO, A)\) — only the competitive entrant enters and the incumbent accepts — and \((OO, F)\) — nobody enters because the incumbent threatens to fight. The second is not sequentially rational: whoever entered, fighting is worse than accepting for the incumbent (\(-1 < 1\) against C, \(0 < 1\) against W). Yet \((OO, F)\) is an SPE, because the only subgame is the whole game. We need a refinement that can evaluate behaviour at information sets that are off the equilibrium path.

title: 13  Perfect Bayesian equilibrium and signaling
text:
13.2 Beliefs and perfect Bayesian equilibrium

Given a BNE, an information set is on the equilibrium path if it is reached with positive probability (given the type distribution), and off the path otherwise. In \((OO, F)\) the incumbent’s information set is off the path.


A system of beliefs \(\mu\) assigns to every information set a probability distribution over its nodes: \(\mu(x)\) is the probability that the player believes they are at node \(x\) when the information set \(h(x)\) is reached.

On the path, beliefs should be conditional probabilities, \(\mu(x) = \Pr[x] / \Pr[h(x)]\) by Bayes’ rule.

A perfect Bayesian equilibrium (PBE) is a pair \((s^*, \mu)\) of a strategy profile and a system of beliefs such that:

every player has beliefs at every information set where they move;
on the equilibrium path, beliefs are derived from \(s^*\) and the prior by Bayes’ rule;
off the equilibrium path, beliefs are arbitrary;
given the beliefs, strategies are sequentially rational: at every information set the player’s continuation strategy is a best response.


A PBE is not just a strategy profile: the beliefs are part of it.

Let \(x_1\) (\(x_2\)) be the incumbent’s node after entry by C (by W), and let the types enter with probabilities \(q_C\), \(q_W\). By Bayes’ rule \[\mu(x_1) = \frac{p\,q_C}{p\,q_C + (1-p)\,q_W}.\] \((EO, A)\) is a PBE with \(\mu(x_1) = 1\): the incumbent knows that an entrant is competitive and accepts. \((OO, F)\) is not: Bayes’ rule cannot be applied (\(q_C = q_W = 0\)), but for any belief Fight is not a best response, so requirement 4 fails. Compare with off-path choices in SPE.


If a profile \(s^*\) (possibly mixed) reaches every information set with positive probability, then \(s^*\) together with the beliefs derived by Bayes’ rule is a PBE if and only if \(s^*\) is a BNE.

text:
13.3 Refinements: sequential equilibrium
The definition above is sometimes called weak PBE because requirement 3 lets off-path beliefs be anything, even inconsistent with the structure of the game.

Nature picks node \(x_1\) or \(x_2\) with probability \(\tfrac12\) each; player 1 does not observe it and chooses U (payoff \(1\) for player 1, game over) or D. After D, player 2 (who doesn’t observe Nature either) chooses L, giving \((2, 2)\) at both nodes, or R, giving \((0, 3)\) at \(x_1\) and \((0, 0)\) at \(x_2\). If player 1 plays D, Bayes’ rule gives \(\mu(x_1) = \tfrac12\); R is then worth \(1.5 < 2\), so L, and D is optimal for player 1: the PBE \((D, L)\). But if player 1 never plays D, any belief is admissible; with \(\mu(x_1) > \tfrac23\), R is optimal, and against R player 1 prefers U. So \((U, R)\) is also a (weak) PBE — supported by the belief that player 1’s non-move somehow reveals Nature’s choice, which player 1 does not even observe.


An assessment \((s^*, \mu)\) is consistent if it is the limit of a sequence \((s^k, \mu^k)\) of fully mixed strategy profiles \(s^k\) and the beliefs \(\mu^k\) derived from them by Bayes’ rule. A sequential equilibrium is a consistent, sequentially rational assessment.

In the odd example, every fully mixed profile gives \(\mu^k(x_1) = \tfrac12\), so consistency forces \(\mu(x_1) = \tfrac12\) and eliminates \((U, R)\). Sequential equilibrium can still be insufficient and is much harder to check; in practice the solution concept is chosen case by case — these distinctions are also useful to argue about how “rational” human behaviour is.

title: 13  Perfect Bayesian equilibrium and signaling
text:
13.4 Signaling games
When the typed player moves first, the move itself may reveal information. If instead only the second mover has types, the first can only guess the reaction from the prior: a screening game (think of a quiz show with a prize behind a screen), where SPE is enough.

A two-player dynamic Bayesian game in which:

Nature chooses the type of player 1 (the sender);
player 1 observes the type and chooses an action (the signal), with at least as many actions as types;
player 2 (the receiver) observes the signal, not the type, updates beliefs, and acts;
player 2 cares about player 1’s type (common values).



In a separating equilibrium different types send different signals, so the signal reveals the type. In a pooling equilibrium all types send the same signal, which carries no information. Hybrid (semi-separating, partially pooling) equilibria have some types randomising so that some signals are partially informative.

Separating equilibria have easy beliefs (each signal points to one type); in pooling equilibria the on-path signal leaves the prior unchanged, while the unused signal is off the path and its beliefs must be chosen to support the equilibrium.

13.4.1 A recipe for pure PBE in signaling games
With two sender types and two messages, there are only four sender strategies to try:

Fix a candidate: pooling (both types send the same message) or separating (they send different ones).
Beliefs on the path follow from Bayes’ rule: after a separating message the type is known; after a pooling message the belief is the prior.
Beliefs off the path (after a message nobody sends) are free in a PBE. Find the range of beliefs that makes the receiver’s prescribed response optimal.
Receiver: check that the response to each message is a best reply to the belief.
Sender: check that no type gains by switching message, given the receiver’s responses.

A pooling candidate survives if some off-path belief deters deviation. A separating candidate needs no off-path beliefs, but each type must prefer its own message.
Revealing (verifiable) actions. Some messages cannot lie: a medical test, a public audit, a costly campaign that exposes the product. After such an action the receiver’s information set is a singleton and backward induction applies directly. Only the non-revealing message needs a belief. The game then shrinks: the receiver has one real decision, and the sender asks whether revealing is worth its cost for each type. Typically the “good” types reveal and the “bad” types stay silent, so silence itself becomes informative (unraveling).

13.5 Worked example: a coffee for Brian
Brian is invited for coffee by his colleague Zoe. His partner Ann is Jealous with probability \(0.8\) or Easygoing with probability \(0.2\). Ann may stay Silent or Trash Zoe; Brian observes the signal and Comes to the coffee or Declines.

Figure: the signaling game in “butterfly” form; payoffs are (Ann, Brian). Brian’s information sets join the nodes after the same signal.
Jealous Ann is deeply hurt if Brian goes; easygoing Ann is only mildly annoyed; trashing Zoe costs Ann \(2\); Brian enjoys the coffee (\(2\)) only if Ann is easygoing and suffers (\(-3\)) if she is jealous.
Step 1: the normal form. Ann’s strategy lists the signal of each type (\(ST\): silent if jealous, trash if easygoing); Brian’s lists the reply to each signal (\(CD\): come after S, decline after T). Careful: Ann’s pair is indexed by types, Brian’s by signals, so filling e.g. \((TS, CD)\) requires matching Brian’s reply to the signal each type sends.

There are five Nash equilibria: three pure, \((SS, DD)\), \((SS, DC)\), \((TT, CD)\), and two mixed, \((TT, \tfrac12 CD + \tfrac12 DD)\) and \((\tfrac16 SS + \tfrac56 TS,\ \tfrac29 CD + \tfrac79 DD)\).
Step 2: beliefs. Let \(\mu_S\) (\(\mu_T\)) be Brian’s belief that Ann is jealous after S (after T). Coming is worth \(-3\mu + 2(1-\mu)\) to Brian, declining \(0\): he comes iff \(\mu \leq 0.4\).

No separating PBE. If Ann played \(ST\), beliefs would be \(\mu_S = 1\), \(\mu_T = 0\) and Brian would reply \(DC\); but against \(DC\) Ann prefers \(SS\). Similarly \(TS\) induces \(CD\), against which Ann prefers \(TT\).
PBE 1: \((SS, DD)\) with \(\mu_S = 0.8\) (the prior, since both types are silent) and off-path \(\mu_T \geq 0.4\) (so that declining after T is optimal). Ann has no reason to trash Zoe since Brian declines anyway.
PBE 2: \((SS, DC)\) with \(\mu_S = 0.8\), \(\mu_T \leq 0.4\): Brian still declines in practice, but would come if Ann trashed Zoe, because he would read it as a sign that she is easygoing.
PBE 3: \((TT, CD)\) with \(\mu_T = 0.8\) and off-path \(\mu_S \leq 0.4\).
PBE 4: Ann plays \(TT\); Brian declines after T (\(\mu_T = 0.8\)); off the path, Brian believes \(\mu_S = 0.4\) — which makes him indifferent — and comes with probability \(q\) after S. Ann must not want to deviate to S: the easygoing type requires \(-q + 3(1-q) \leq 1\), i.e. \(q \geq \tfrac12\). So this is a continuum of PBE (with \(q = 1\) recovering PBE 3); note that \((TT, DD)\) itself is not an equilibrium.
PBE 5 (semi-separating): easygoing Ann is always silent; jealous Ann is silent with probability \(\tfrac16\). T is sent only by the jealous type, so \(\mu_T = 1\) and Brian declines. After S, Bayes’ rule gives \[\mu_S = \frac{0.8 \cdot \tfrac16}{0.8 \cdot \tfrac16 + 0.2} = 0.4,\] exactly the value that makes Brian indifferent, so he can mix. He comes with probability \(\tfrac29\) after S, which makes jealous Ann indifferent between S (\(-6 \cdot \tfrac29 + 3 \cdot \tfrac79 = 1\)) and T (\(1\)).







The recipe for signaling games: (1) write the normal form, minding the type/signal indexing; (2) find all NE; (3) for each, compute on-path beliefs by Bayes’ rule and find off-path beliefs that make the receiver’s prescribed replies optimal — if none exist, the NE is not a PBE.

text:
13.6 Education as a signal and the intuitive criterion
Spence’s (1973) job-market model shows how a costly action can transmit information even when it is useless in itself. A worker is of High productivity (\(2\)) with probability \(p\) or Low (\(1\)). Before being hired, the worker chooses an education level \(e \geq 0\), which costs \(e\) to a Low type and \(e/2\) to a High type. Competitive employers pay the expected productivity given their belief after observing \(e\).

Separating PBE. High chooses \(e^*\) and Low chooses \(0\); the wage is \(2\) after \(e^*\) and \(1\) otherwise. Low must not mimic, \(1 \geq 2 - e^*\); High must prefer to signal, \(2 - e^*/2 \geq 1\). Any \(e^* \in [1, 2]\) works, supported by the belief “anyone with \(e < e^*\) is Low”.
Pooling PBE. Both choose \(e = 0\) and receive \(\bar w = 1 + p\), with pessimistic beliefs off the path.

Perfect Bayesian equilibrium allows any belief after an unexpected action, hence the multiplicity. The intuitive criterion (Cho and Kreps, 1987) asks: could this deviation possibly benefit this type? If a deviation can only benefit one type, the responder should believe it comes from that type.

In the separating family, an education level \(e \in (1, e^*)\) would never pay for a Low worker (even with wage \(2\), \(2 - e < 1\)), but would pay for a High one. So the beliefs “\(e < e^*\) means Low” are unreasonable, and only the least-cost separating equilibrium \(e^* = 1\) survives (the Riley outcome).
The pooling equilibrium always fails the criterion (for \(p < 1\)). Any \(e \in (1 - p,\ 2(1 - p))\) cannot benefit Low even at wage \(2\) (\(2 - e < 1 + p\)), but if read as High it gives High \(2 - e/2 > 1 + p\).

The lessons generalise: signals work because they are costlier for the types you want to separate from (single crossing), and equilibrium refinements select the cheapest credible signal. In networks the same logic underlies proof-of-work, costly authentication and reputation deposits.

text:
13.7 Reputation building
In a finitely repeated Prisoner’s Dilemma the unique SPE is to defect always. A little uncertainty about types changes this dramatically (Kreps, Milgrom, Roberts and Wilson, 1982).
Stage payoffs are \((C,C) = (1,1)\), \((C,D) = (-1,2)\), \((D,C) = (2,-1)\), \((D,D) = (0,0)\). Player B is strategic. Player A is a grim-trigger type with probability \(p\) (cooperates until B defects, then defects forever) or strategic with probability \(1 - p\).

Two rounds. In round 2 strategic players defect. In round 1 strategic A defects, and B, cooperating, gets \(p(1) + (1-p)(-1)\) in round 1 plus \(2p\) in round 2 (exploiting the grim-trigger type, who still cooperates): total \(4p - 1\). Defecting gives \(2p\) (round 1) and \(0\) after. B cooperates in round 1 iff \(p > \tfrac12\).
Three rounds. If \(p > \tfrac12\), the unique PBE has both B and the strategic A cooperating in round 1. Strategic A pools with the grim-trigger type: by cooperating he keeps B’s belief at \(p > \tfrac12\), so B keeps cooperating in round 2, and A earns \(1 + 2 + 0\) instead of \(2 + 0 + 0\) from revealing himself. B, in turn, cooperates in round 1 even if he expected the strategic A to defect, since \(5p - 1 > 2p\) for \(p > \tfrac13\).

Strategic players build a reputation: they defect at the end, but to an outside observer they cooperate. In general, in a \(T\)-stage game the number of rounds in which a strategic player defects is bounded by a constant depending on \(p\) but not on \(T\).
The tough negotiator. In an ultimatum game the proposer offers a High share (payoffs \((2,1)\) if accepted) or a Moderate one (\((1,2)\)); refusal gives \((0,0)\). The unique SPE is \((H, \text{always accept})\). Now let the responder be a “jerk” with probability \(p\), who finds H worse than nothing (payoff \(-1\)). In one round the proposer offers H iff \(2(1-p) > 1\), i.e. \(p < \tfrac12\). With a second round (after a refusal the proposer offers again, payoffs discounted by \(\delta\)) the game becomes intractable in normal form — the responder has \(2^{12}\) strategies — but sequential rationality reduces it. With \(\delta = 0.9\) and \(p = 0.1\) the unique PBE is semi-separating: H is always offered first; the jerk always refuses; a normal responder refuses with probability \(\tfrac19\) (so that after a refusal \(\mu_H = \Pr[\text{jerk} \mid \text{refusal}] = \tfrac12\), making the proposer indifferent between H, worth \(2\delta(1-\mu_H)\), and M, worth \(\delta\)); in round 2 the proposer repeats H with probability \(\tfrac89\) (making the normal responder indifferent: \(\delta[\tfrac89 \cdot 1 + \tfrac19 \cdot 2] = 1\)). Even an unlikely “tough” type gives the responder bargaining power: a normal responder sometimes mimics it.

title: 13  Perfect Bayesian equilibrium and signaling
text:
13.8 Cheap talk
In cheap talk (Crawford and Sobel, 1982), Nature reveals a state \(t\) to player 1 only; player 1 sends a message that costs nothing and has no direct effect on payoffs; player 2 then acts. The question is how much information costless messages can transmit when interests are not aligned.

Player 2 found a job in city A and chooses where to live, \(a \in \{1, \dots, 5\}\) (1 = city A, 5 = city B where player 1 lives). The best location depends on traffic conditions \(t \in \{1, 3, 5\}\), equally likely and known only to player 1. Player 2’s payoff is \(5 - (t - a)^2\); player 1 is biased towards having the friend close: \(5 - (t + b - a)^2\) with \(b = 1.1\).

No truthful PBE. If messages were believed, the type \(t = 3\) would claim “5”: the friend would choose \(a = 5\), giving player 1 \(5 - 0.81 = 4.19\) instead of \(5 - 1.21 = 3.79\).
A babbling PBE always exists: messages are uninformative and player 2 chooses \(a = 3\) from the prior.
A partially informative PBE: player 1 reports \(t = 1\) truthfully but pools \(t \in \{3, 5\}\) into “high”. Player 2 then chooses \(a = 1\) or \(a = 4\). Type 1 prefers the truth (\(3.79\) vs. \(1.39\)); types 3 and 5 prefer “high”.


With a continuous state \(t \in [0, 1]\) and quadratic losses, there is never a truthful equilibrium, there is always a babbling one, and a two-message (threshold) equilibrium exists iff the bias is small enough (\(b < \tfrac14\) for uniform \(t\)). Applications include legislative committees and expert advisers: with the decision maker’s payoff \(-(t - a)^2\), \(t \sim \mathcal U[-w, w]\), and the adviser’s \(-(t + b - a)^2\), informative advice (under open or closed rules) is possible only if \(b \leq w\).






The “negative” results of cheap talk justify a common engineering practice: protocols exchange coarse information — congested / not congested, low / high battery — rather than exact values. With slightly misaligned incentives, more detail would not be credible anyway.

text:
13.9 Exercises
Problems from Badia and Marchioro (BM), Chapter 6.

(BM 6.6) Mark buys trousers Immediately at €50 or Waits, in which case Nadia Keeps the price or Lowers it to €30 at the end of the week. Mark values them at €100. Late transactions are discounted by \(\delta = 0.8\). Nadia’s cost is €20 with probability \(0.75\) (and lowering the price then also brings €20 of goodwill, not discounted) or €35. Find the BNE and the SPE.


Solution. Nadia’s strategies are (cost 20, cost 35). Waiting gives Mark \(40\) (K) or \(56\) (L). It gives Nadia \(24\) (K) or \(28\) (L) at cost 20, and \(12\) (K) or \(-4\) (L) at cost 35. Buying immediately gives Mark \(50\) and Nadia \(30\) or \(15\). Normal form, Mark W against KK, KL, LK, LL: \((40, 21)\), \((44, 17)\), \((52, 24)\), \((56, 20)\); Mark I: \((50, 26.25)\). BNE: \((I, KK)\), \((I, KL)\), \((W, LK)\). Sequential rationality requires L at cost 20 and K at cost 35, so Nadia plays LK. Then Mark waits (\(52 > 50\)). The unique SPE is \((W, LK)\). (The printed payoffs contain small arithmetic slips; the equilibria are unchanged.)


(BM 6.7) Janine brings food from Home (payoff \(2\); stand \(0\)) or Eats at the stand. The worker there is Alfred (\(0.8\)) or Brianna (\(0.2\)) and Gives a sandwich (Janine \(5\), worker \(1\)) or Denies it (Janine \(0\), worker \(0\); but Brianna, who dislikes Janine, gets \(5\)). Find the BNE and the SPE.


Solution. The stand’s strategies are (Alfred, Brianna). E against GG, GD, DG, DD gives \((5, 1)\), \((4, 1.8)\), \((1, 0.2)\), \((0, 1)\); H gives \((2, 0)\). BNE: \((E, GD)\), \((H, DG)\), \((H, DD)\). Sequential rationality: Alfred gives, Brianna denies, so GD, and Janine eats (\(4 > 2\)). SPE \((E, GD)\); the other two rest on Alfred threatening to deny. (The printed expected payoffs of the stand are slightly off: \(1.8\), not \(2.8\).)


(BM 6.8) Riccardo is infected with probability \(0.2\). At the border he takes a Swab (revealing his status; cost \(10\)) or Talks. The officer Admits or Denies. Riccardo gets \(20\) if admitted, \(0\) otherwise. The officer gets \(5\) for admitting a healthy traveller, \(-50\) for an infected one, \(0\) for denying. Find the PBE and classify it.


Solution. After a swab the officer knows the type: he admits the healthy (Riccardo \(10\)) and denies the infected (\(-10\)). After T, let \(\mu\) be the officer’s belief that Riccardo is infected; admitting pays \(5 - 55\mu\), so he admits iff \(\mu \leq 1/11\). The infected type never swabs (\(-10 < 0\)). If the healthy type talked too (pooling), \(\mu = 0.2 > 1/11\) and the officer would deny, so the healthy type would rather swab (\(10 > 0\)). PBE: infected Talks, healthy Swabs, the officer believes \(\mu(T) = 1\) and Denies after T, and admits after a negative swab. It is separating: the costly swab is the signal only the healthy type is willing to send.


(BM 6.9) John and Mary exchange gifts at Christmas and on Valentine’s Day (two rounds, \(\delta = 1\)): a gift costs the giver \(5\) and is worth \(12\) to the receiver. Mary is strategic. With probability \(p\) John is a tit-for-tat type (gives at Christmas, then copies Mary); otherwise he is strategic. (a) Payoffs if \(p = 0\)? (b) Probability that John does not give at Christmas? (c) When does Mary give at Christmas?


Solution. 

A twice-repeated Prisoner’s Dilemma: \((N, N)\) twice, payoffs \(0\). (b) Only the strategic John withholds at Christmas: probability \(1 - p\). (c) Mary never gives on Valentine’s Day (the last round). If she withholds at Christmas she gets \(12p\) (the tit-for-tat John’s Christmas gift). If she gives, she gets \(p(12 - 5 + 12) - 5(1 - p) = 24p - 5\): tit-for-tat John rewards her on Valentine’s Day. She gives iff \(24p - 5 > 12p\), i.e. \(p > 5/12\). A modest probability of a reciprocating type makes even a selfish player cooperate early: the seed of the reputation results of Kreps–Milgrom–Roberts–Wilson.



(BM 6.10) A clerk Stays put (bandit \(100\), clerk \(0\)) or Punches a bandit whose gun is fake with probability \(p\). After a punch the bandit Reacts or Flees. Fake gun and react: both \(-10\). Real gun and react: clerk \(-100\), bandit \(80\). Flee: clerk \(10\), bandit \(0\). Find the BNE as a function of \(p\) and the SPE.


Solution. The bandit’s strategies are (fake, real). P against RR, RF, FR, FF: clerk \(90p - 100\), \(10 - 20p\), \(110p - 100\), \(10\). S gives \(0\) against everything. Sequential rationality: flee with a fake gun (\(0 > -10\)) and react with a real one (\(80 > 0\)), i.e. FR. The clerk punches iff \(110p - 100 \geq 0\), i.e. \(p \geq 10/11\). BNE: \((S, RR)\) for all \(p\); \((S, RF)\) for \(p \geq 1/2\); \((S, FR)\) for \(p \leq 10/11\); \((P, FR)\) for \(p \geq 10/11\). Only those with FR are SPE. The clerk should play the hero only if he is almost sure the gun is fake.


(BM 6.12) A start-up’s gadget is Effective or Useless (probability \(\tfrac12\) each). It runs a Campaign (cost \(20\), reveals the type) or keeps a Low profile. The incumbent Fights or Yields. Yield: \(50\) each. Fight: \((80, 0)\) if Effective, \((0, 80)\) if Useless. Find the PBE.


Solution. After a campaign the incumbent yields to an effective gadget (\(50 > 0\)) and fights a useless one (\(80 > 50\)), so C yields \(30\) (effective) or \(-20\) (useless). After L, with belief \(\mu = \Pr(\text{effective})\), fighting pays \(80(1 - \mu)\) against \(50\) for yielding. Normal form (start-up strategies (effective, useless), incumbent’s answer to L): CC \((5, 65)\) for both answers; CL \((15, 65)\) / \((40, 50)\); LC \((30, 40)\) / \((15, 65)\); LL \((40, 40)\) / \((50, 50)\). LL is strictly dominant. With \(\mu = 1/2\) the incumbent yields (\(50 > 40\)). Pooling PBE: both types keep a low profile, the incumbent believes the prior after L and yields. The campaign is too expensive to be worth revealing even good news.


(BM 6.16) A student’s green pass is valid (\(0.9\)) or fake (\(0.1\)). The student Displays or Hides it; the professor Admits or sends Online, unable to tell fakes apart. Valid: admitted \((10, 10)\); displayed but sent online: professor \(-50\); otherwise \(0\). Fake: admitted after display \((-100, -100)\); admitted without display \((-50, -200)\); displayed and sent online: student \(-200\); otherwise \(0\). Find the pure PBE.


Solution. Student strategies (valid, fake), professor strategies (after D, after H). The pure NE are \((DH, AO)\) and \((HH, OO)\). Separating \((DH, AO)\): valid passes are displayed, fakes hidden. Beliefs \(\mu(\text{valid} \mid D) = 1\) and \(\mu(\text{valid} \mid H) = 0\); admitting after D and sending online after H are optimal. Pooling \((HH, OO)\): nobody displays, and \(\mu(\text{valid} \mid H) = 0.9\) makes O optimal (\(0 > 0.9\cdot10 - 0.1\cdot200 = -11\)). D is off the path, so its belief is free. Admitting after D pays \(110\mu - 100\) and online pays \(-50\mu\), so O after D is optimal iff \(\mu(\text{valid} \mid D) \leq 5/8\). The pooling PBE needs pessimistic off-path beliefs. By the intuitive criterion, displaying could only benefit the valid type, so the pooling equilibrium is not reasonable.

From the course material:

A young cowboy Y, insulted by an outlaw O, can let it slide (\((-20, 0)\)) or challenge O. O can apologise (\((10, -10)\)) or duel. If O is a sharpshooter (prior \(p\)) the duel gives \((-100, 20)\); otherwise each wins with probability \(\tfrac12\), the winner getting \(20\) and the loser \(-100\). Find the PBE for \(p = 0.2\).


Solution. For a non-sharpshooter the duel is worth \(\tfrac12 \cdot 20 + \tfrac12(-100) = -40\) to both players. Sequential rationality: a sharpshooter duels (\(20 > -10\)); a fake apologises (\(-10 > -40\)). Then challenging gives Y \(p(-100) + (1-p)(10) = 0.2(-100) + 0.8 \cdot 10 = -12 > -20\), so Y challenges. The unique PBE (indeed the unique SPE of the type-agent tree) is: Y challenges; a sharpshooter O duels, a fake O apologises. Y would let it slide only if \(-100p + 10(1-p) < -20\), i.e. \(p > 3/11 \approx 0.27\). This is a screening game — the uninformed player moves first and O knows his own type — so beliefs are trivial and SPE suffices; in normal form there is also a NE in which Y lets it slide and O threatens to duel whatever his type, but it is not sequentially rational.


In the coffee game, check that \((TT, DD)\) is not a Nash equilibrium and explain in words why PBE 4 needs Brian to come after S with probability at least \(\tfrac12\).


Solution. Against \(DD\), Ann gets \(3\) from \(SS\) and \(1\) from \(TT\): she deviates to silence. In PBE 4 Brian’s reply to the off-path signal S must deter both types from switching to S. The jealous type gets \(-6q + 3(1-q) \leq 1\) iff \(q \geq \tfrac29\); the easygoing type gets \(-q + 3(1-q) \leq 1\) iff \(q \geq \tfrac12\). The binding constraint is the easygoing type’s, hence \(q \geq \tfrac12\).

title: 14  Auctions and mechanism design
text:
14.1 Sealed-bid auctions
So far the game was given and we predicted its outcome. Mechanism design reverses the question: a designer wants a certain outcome — the good goes to whoever values it most, a protocol allocates bandwidth efficiently — and must design the game so that self-interested players with private information produce it in equilibrium. Auctions are the most important example, and the second-price auction shows that a well-designed game can make telling the truth a dominant strategy. The revelation principle then tells us where to look for good mechanisms.

title: 14  Auctions and mechanism design
text:
One seller and \(N\) bidders; bidder \(i\) privately values the object \(v_i \geq 0\). Each bidder submits a bid \(b_i \geq 0\) without seeing the others. The highest bid wins; ties are broken by sharing (or by a coin flip).


14.1.1 First-price auction
The winner pays their own bid. With \(W\) tied winners, \[u_i(b) = \begin{cases} v_i - b_i & \text{if } i \text{ is the only highest bidder}, \\ (v_i - b_i)/W & \text{if } i \text{ is among } W > 1 \text{ highest bidders}, \\ 0 & \text{otherwise}. \end{cases}\]

Bidding \(b_i \geq v_i\) always yields \(u_i \leq 0\), so it is weakly dominated by bidding below \(v_i\).
Bidding \(b_i = 0\) wins only if everyone bids \(0\), and is weakly dominated by a small positive bid.
Between two bids \(0 < b_i < b_i' < v_i\) nothing can be said in general: against opponents bidding \(0\) the lower bid is better, against opponents bidding \((b_i + b_i')/2\) the higher one is.

Rational bidders shade their bids below their value. With incomplete information one computes the Bayesian Nash equilibrium: for two bidders with values independent and uniform on \([0, 1]\), the symmetric BNE is \(b(v) = v/2\). Indeed, if the opponent bids \(v_j/2\), bidding \(b\) wins with probability \(\Pr[v_j/2 < b] = 2b\), and \(\max_b (v - b)\,2b\) gives \(b = v/2\). (With \(N\) bidders, \(b(v) = \tfrac{N-1}{N} v\).)


14.1.2 Second-price (Vickrey) auction
Proposed by Vickrey (1961): the highest bidder wins but pays the second-highest bid \(S = \max_{j \neq i} b_j\): \[u_i(b) = \begin{cases} v_i - S & \text{if } b_i > S, \\ (v_i - S)/W & \text{if } b_i = S \text{ with } W \text{ tied winners}, \\ 0 & \text{if } b_i < S. \end{cases}\]

In a second-price auction, bidding \(b_i = v_i\) weakly dominates every other bid.

Proof. Compare \(v_i\) with a lower bid \(b_i < v_i\), for each value of \(S\):

\(S < b_i\): both bids win alone and pay \(S\): same payoff \(v_i - S\).
\(S = b_i\): \(b_i\) ties and gets \((v_i - S)/W\); \(v_i\) wins alone and gets \(v_i - S > (v_i - S)/W\).
\(b_i < S < v_i\): \(b_i\) loses (\(0\)), \(v_i\) wins (\(v_i - S > 0\)).
\(S \geq v_i\): \(b_i\) loses (\(0\)); \(v_i\) loses or ties at zero surplus (\(0\)).

Now a higher bid \(b_i > v_i\):

\(S < v_i\): both win and pay \(S\): same payoff.
\(S = v_i\): both get \(0\).
\(v_i < S\): \(v_i\) loses (\(0\)); \(b_i\) either loses (\(0\)) or wins/ties paying \(S > v_i\) (negative payoff).

In every case \(v_i\) is at least as good, and strictly better in some. \(\square\)
So \((v_1, \dots, v_n)\) is a Nash equilibrium (in dominant strategies — no beliefs needed), and the second-price auction makes bidders reveal their true values. In a first-price auction, by contrast, bidding \(v_i\) always gives \(0\) and is dominated.
Efficiency. Social surplus is maximised if the object goes to the bidder with the highest value. In the second-price auction this bidder wins and pays \(S\): the bidder gets \(v - S\), the seller \(S\), total \(v\) — Pareto efficient. For the first-price auction with symmetric bidders the BNE is also efficient (bids are increasing in values), and with independent private values the two formats yield the same expected revenue: for two uniform bidders, \(\mathbb E[\max_i v_i]/2 = \tfrac13 = \mathbb E[\min_i v_i]\) (the revenue equivalence theorem).

title: 14  Auctions and mechanism design
text:
14.2 Revenue equivalence and reserve prices
First-price bidders shade their bids and second-price bidders do not, but the winner of a second-price auction pays only the second-highest value. Which raises more money? With \(N\) bidders and i.i.d. values uniform on \([0, 1]\), both give expected revenue \(\frac{N-1}{N+1}\). This is no coincidence:

With risk-neutral bidders and independent private values from a common continuous distribution, every auction format in which (i) the highest-value bidder always wins and (ii) a bidder with the lowest possible value expects zero payment yields the same expected revenue and the same expected payment for each type.

The reason is the envelope theorem. A type’s equilibrium utility grows with its value at a rate equal to its winning probability, which is fixed by (i). Payments are then pinned down by (ii). First-price, second-price, English, Dutch, all-pay and even third-price auctions (where bidders bid above their values) all raise \(\frac{N-1}{N+1}\) in the uniform case. Revenue equivalence fails with risk-averse bidders (first-price then raises more, as shading is risky), with asymmetric bidders, and with correlated or common values.
Reserve prices. The seller can beat every efficient format by refusing to sell below a reserve \(r\). With two uniform bidders and a second-price auction, revenue is \(R(r) = \frac{1 + 3r^2 - 4r^3}{3}\), maximised at \(r^* = \tfrac12\) with \(R = \tfrac5{12} > \tfrac13\). The seller gives up some efficient trades (when both values are below \(\tfrac12\)) to extract more from a lone high bidder. In general \(r^*\) solves \(r - \frac{1 - F(r)}{f(r)} = 0\) (zero virtual value), independently of the number of bidders.

title: 14  Auctions and mechanism design
section: 14.3 Common values and the winner’s curse
text:
14.3 Common values and the winner’s curse
When the object has the same, unknown value for everyone (an oil tract, a spectrum licence), each bidder holds a noisy estimate. Winning is bad news: it means your estimate was the most optimistic. A bidder who bids as if their own estimate were the truth overpays systematically — the winner’s curse. Rational bidders condition on winning, \(\mathbb E[V \mid \text{my signal}, \text{I win}]\), and shade more as the number of competitors grows. Revenue equivalence breaks down here: open ascending auctions, which reveal others’ information as bidders drop out, raise more revenue than sealed bids (the linkage principle).

title: 14  Auctions and mechanism design
text:
14.4 Vickrey–Clarke–Groves auctions
A VCG auction extends the second-price idea to several items. Each bidder submits a value for every combination of items; the seller chooses the allocation maximising the total declared value (possibly a hard combinatorial problem); then each winner pays for the harm they cause to the others: \[p_i = \underbrace{V(\mathcal N \setminus \{i\})}_{\substack{\text{others' best total value}\\ \text{without } i}} \;-\; \underbrace{V_{-i}(x^*)}_{\substack{\text{others' value in the}\\ \text{chosen allocation}}} .\]

A bids \(5\) for a single item, B bids \(4\) for a single item, C bids \(7\) for the pair only. The optimal allocation gives one item to A and one to B (total \(9 > 7\)). Without A, the best the others could do is C taking both (\(7\)); in the chosen allocation the others get \(4\) (B). So A pays \(7 - 4 = 3\). Symmetrically B pays \(7 - 5 = 2\), and C, who wins nothing and harms nobody, pays \(0\).

VCG mechanisms are truthful: bidding one’s true valuations is weakly dominant, for the same reason as in the Vickrey auction — a bidder’s report affects only the allocation, never the price conditional on the allocation, and the allocation maximises the bidder’s own utility plus a term they cannot affect. Yet VCG is rare in practice: revenue can be low (even zero), it is non-monotone (adding bidders can lower revenue), and it is vulnerable to collusion and shill bidding.

title: 14  Auctions and mechanism design
text:
14.5 Mechanism design
Players \(1, \dots, n\) must choose among public alternatives \(X\). Their preferences depend on private types \(t = (t_1, \dots, t_n) \in T = T_1 \times \dots \times T_n\), the state of the world; types are private, the prior is common knowledge. Payoffs are quasi-linear in money, \[v_i(x, t_i, m_i) = u_i(x, t_i) + m_i ,\] where \(m_i\) is a monetary transfer.

A choice rule is a map \(f : T \to Y\), with \(Y = \{(x, m_1, \dots, m_n) : x \in X,\ \sum_i m_i \leq 0\}\). It consists of a decision rule \(x(t)\) and a transfer rule \(m(t)\); the budget constraint says the designer does not inject money.

The designer would like to implement \(f\), but does not know \(t\), and players might lie.

A mechanism \(\Gamma = (A_1, \dots, A_n; g)\) specifies an action set \(A_i\) for each player and an outcome function \(g : A_1 \times \dots \times A_n \to Y\). In the induced Bayesian game a pure strategy is \(s_i : T_i \to A_i\). The mechanism implements \(f\) (in BNE) if it has a Bayesian Nash equilibrium \(s^*\) with \(g(s^*(t)) = f(t)\) for every \(t \in T\).


Figure: a mechanism implements \(f\) if equilibrium play \(s^*\) followed by the outcome function \(g\) reproduces \(f\).

title: 14  Auctions and mechanism design
text:
14.6 The revelation principle

A mechanism is a direct revelation mechanism if \(A_i = T_i\) for every \(i\) and \(g = f\): the designer simply asks players to report their types and applies the choice rule. \(f\) is truthfully implementable in BNE if truth-telling, \(s_i^*(t_i) = t_i\) for all \(i\) and \(t_i\), is a BNE of its direct revelation mechanism.


A choice rule \(f\) is implementable by some mechanism if and only if it is truthfully implementable in Bayesian Nash equilibrium.

Proof. (\(\Leftarrow\)) The direct mechanism is a mechanism. (\(\Rightarrow\)) Let \(\Gamma\) implement \(f\) through the equilibrium \(s^*\). Build a direct mechanism that, on reports \(\hat t\), computes \(g(s^*(\hat t))\): it “plays the equilibrium on behalf of” each player. If some type gained by misreporting \(\hat t_i\), the same type would have gained in \(\Gamma\) by playing \(s_i^*(\hat t_i)\) instead of \(s_i^*(t_i)\), contradicting that \(s^*\) is an equilibrium. \(\square\)
The consequence is powerful: to know whether any clever mechanism can achieve \(f\), it suffices to check whether truth-telling is an equilibrium of the direct one. If the direct mechanism fails, no other mechanism will work. VCG mechanisms are exactly direct mechanisms in which truth-telling is even dominant.






In ICT, “mechanisms” are protocols: a scheduler asking users to declare their traffic demand, a spectrum auction, a crowdsensing platform paying for reported measurements. The revelation principle says one can restrict attention to protocols that ask for the private information directly and pay so that reporting it honestly is in each user’s interest.

title: 14  Auctions and mechanism design
text:
14.7 Exercises
Badia and Marchioro’s handbook has no auction problems; these are from Tadelis (T), Chapters 13–14.

(T 13.2) In a second-price auction with complete information (everyone knows all values), is bidding one’s value still weakly dominant? Are there other NE?


Solution. Yes: dominance compares payoffs profile by profile, so information about the others is irrelevant. But there are many other NE. For example, the bidder with the lowest value bids above the highest value and everyone else bids \(0\). The low bidder wins at price \(0\); anyone else could win only by outbidding, paying more than their value. Such equilibria are in weakly dominated strategies and are inefficient.


(T 13.3) Two bidders with values in \(\{0, 1, 2\}\) (equally likely, independent) face a second-price auction with reserve \(r\): if only one bid reaches \(r\) that bidder pays \(r\); if none does, the good is not sold. (a) Is truthful bidding still dominant? (b)–(c) Expected revenue for \(r = 0\) and \(r = 1\)? (d) The optimal \(r\)?


Solution. 

Yes: the reserve acts like an extra bid by the seller. (b) Revenue is the lower value: \(\mathbb E[\min] = 1\cdot\tfrac39 + 2\cdot\tfrac19 = \tfrac59\). (c) With \(r = 1\): if both values are \(\geq 1\) (probability \(4/9\)), the minimum is paid, contributing \(\tfrac59\); if exactly one is \(\geq 1\) (\(4/9\)), that bidder pays \(1\), contributing \(\tfrac49\). Total \(1\). (d) For \(r \in (1, 2]\) revenue is \(\tfrac19\cdot2 + \tfrac49 r\), maximised at \(r = 2\): \(\tfrac{10}9\), double the no-reserve revenue. (Above \(2\) nothing sells.) The reserve extracts the full value from a lone high bidder, at the cost of never selling to two low ones.



(T 13.4) Two bidders with values uniform on \([0, 1]\); second-price auction with reserve \(r\). Show that \(r = 0\) is not optimal and find the optimal \(r\).


Solution. Revenue: if both values exceed \(r\) the seller gets \(\min(v_1, v_2)\); if exactly one does, \(r\). Integrating, \(R(r) = \frac{1 + 3r^2 - 4r^3}{3}\). \(R'(r) = 2r - 4r^2 > 0\) for \(0 < r < \tfrac12\), so a small reserve raises revenue (the loss, not selling when both values are tiny, is second order). The optimum is \(r^* = \tfrac12\) with \(R = \tfrac5{12}\), versus \(\tfrac13\) without a reserve; a simulation with \(10^6\) draws gives \(0.4167\).


(T 13.5) First-price auction, two bidders with values \(4\) or \(8\) (probability \(\tfrac12\) each). Show that the low type bids \(4\) and the high type mixes on \([4, 6]\); find the mixture and the seller’s revenue, and compare with an English auction.


Solution. A low type bidding below \(4\) would be overbid by the other low type at no cost, so \(b_L = 4\) (zero surplus). The high type wins against a low rival by bidding just above \(4\), earning \(8 - 4 = 4\) with probability \(\tfrac12\), so its equilibrium payoff is \(2\). A bid \(b\) must give the same: \((8 - b)\bigl(\tfrac12 + \tfrac12F(b)\bigr) = 2\), so \[F(b) = \frac{b - 4}{8 - b}, \qquad b \in [4, 6].\] The support ends where \(F = 1\), at \(b = 6\). (Tadelis states “uniformly”, but uniform bids are not optimal: e.g. \(b = 5\) would give \(2.25\).) Expected high bid \(8 - 4\ln2 = 5.23\), expected maximum of two high bids \(5.55\). Revenue: \(\tfrac14\cdot4 + \tfrac12\cdot5.23 + \tfrac14\cdot5.55 = 5\). An English auction sells at the second-highest value: \(\tfrac34\cdot4 + \tfrac14\cdot8 = 5\). Revenue equivalence holds even with discrete types here.


(T 13.6) In a third-price auction (\(n \geq 3\) bidders, values uniform on \([0, 1]\); the highest bid wins and pays the third-highest bid), verify that \(s(\theta) = \frac{n-1}{n-2}\theta\) is a symmetric BNE, explain overbidding, and compute the revenue.


Solution. Bidding above value is harmless in the event that matters: winning is good whenever the price (the third-highest bid) is below your value. The second-highest bid is irrelevant to the price, which raises the value of winning. Checking the first-order condition of the expected payoff under the candidate strategy confirms \(s(\theta) = \frac{n-1}{n-2}\theta\). Revenue: \(\frac{n-1}{n-2}\,\mathbb E[\theta_{(3)}] = \frac{n-1}{n-2}\cdot\frac{n-2}{n+1} = \frac{n-1}{n+1}\), the same as first- and second-price auctions, as revenue equivalence predicts.


(T 14.1, Brothers) Brother 1 ranks \(A \succ B \succ C\). Brother 2 is type \(\theta'\) (\(C \succ B \succ A\)) or \(\theta''\) (\(B \succ A \succ C\)). The parents ask brother 2 to report his type and implement \(f(\theta') = B\), \(f(\theta'') = A\). Is truth-telling dominant? What if \(f(\theta') = C\), \(f(\theta'') = A\)? Or \(f \equiv B\)?


Solution. 

Type \(\theta''\) gets \(A\) by telling the truth but \(B\), which he prefers, by lying. Not incentive compatible. (b) \(\theta'\) gets his favourite \(C\); \(\theta''\) gets \(A\) truthfully versus \(C\) by lying, and prefers \(A\). Truth-telling is dominant. (c) A constant choice is trivially incentive compatible, but it ignores the information. This is the revelation principle in miniature: a social choice function is implementable iff no type gains by imitating another.


From the course material:

Three bidders with values \(10\), \(7\), \(4\) participate in a second-price auction. What are the dominant-strategy outcome and the seller’s revenue? Show that bidder 2 cannot gain by bidding \(12\).


Solution. Truthful bids: bidder 1 wins and pays \(7\); revenue \(7\), bidder 1’s surplus \(3\). If bidder 2 bids \(12\), he wins and pays \(10 > 7 = v_2\): payoff \(-3 < 0\).


In a first-price auction with \(N\) bidders whose values are i.i.d. uniform on \([0,1]\), verify that \(b(v) = \frac{N-1}{N} v\) is a symmetric BNE and compute the expected revenue.


Solution. If the others bid \(\frac{N-1}{N} v_j\), bidding \(b\) wins iff all \(v_j < \frac{N}{N-1} b\), with probability \(\bigl(\frac{N b}{N-1}\bigr)^{N-1}\). Maximising \((v - b) b^{N-1}\) gives \((N-1)(v - b) = b\), i.e. \(b = \frac{N-1}{N} v\). Revenue: \(\frac{N-1}{N}\,\mathbb E[\max v] = \frac{N-1}{N}\cdot\frac{N}{N+1} = \frac{N-1}{N+1}\), equal to the expected second-highest value — revenue equivalence.

title: 15  Coalitions and axiomatic bargaining
text:
15.1 Coalitional games
Non-cooperative game theory models each player’s choices and asks what is self-enforcing. Cooperation then has to emerge — through repetition, reputation or punishment. Cooperative game theory takes a different stance: it assumes that players can sign binding agreements and asks which agreements are stable and which are fair. Its two main instruments are coalitional games, where groups of players generate value to be shared, and axiomatic bargaining, where a sensible split is characterised by a list of desirable properties rather than by a bargaining procedure.
Transferable utility means \(v(S)\) can be split arbitrarily (think of money). In non-transferable utility (NTU) games, coalition members know in advance what each gets, and \(v(S)\) is replaced by a set of achievable payoff vectors.
The set \(\mathcal N\) is the grand coalition. Whether it forms — whether everybody cooperates — depends on how \(v(\mathcal N)\) is split: equal shares, proportional shares, the Shapley value, the nucleolus. A player who deems their share too small may leave.
In a superadditive game cooperation is always beneficial and the grand coalition maximises total value; the question is how to split it so that nobody wants to leave.

title: 15  Coalitions and axiomatic bargaining
text:
A coalitional (TU) game is a pair \((\mathcal N, v)\): a set of players \(\mathcal N\) and a characteristic function \(v : 2^{\mathcal N} \to \mathbb R\) with \(v(\emptyset) = 0\). A coalition is any \(S \subseteq \mathcal N\); \(v(S)\) is the total value its members can generate on their own. Each player’s action is the coalition to join (a loner joins \(\{i\}\)), and the value of a coalition is split among its members as payoffs \(x_i\) with \(\sum_{i \in S} x_i = v(S)\).



A coalitional game is simple if \(v(S) \in \{0, 1\}\) for every \(S\): coalitions are winning or losing (weighted voting, committees). A veto player belongs to every winning coalition; a dictator is a veto player whose singleton coalition is winning.



\((\mathcal N, v)\) is superadditive if \(v(S_1 \cup S_2) \geq v(S_1) + v(S_2)\) for all disjoint \(S_1, S_2\).

title: 15  Coalitions and axiomatic bargaining
text:
15.2 The core

The core is the set of allocations \((x_1, \dots, x_n)\) such that \[\sum_{i \in \mathcal N} x_i = v(\mathcal N) \quad \text{(efficiency)}, \qquad \sum_{i \in S} x_i \geq v(S) \quad \forall\, S \subseteq \mathcal N \quad \text{(coalitional rationality)}.\]

No coalition can do better by breaking away: a non-empty core means a stable grand coalition. Drawbacks: the core is often empty; sometimes it is very large; and core allocations may be unfair.

A collection of weights \(\alpha(S) \geq 0\), \(S \neq \emptyset\), is balanced if \(\sum_{S \ni i} \alpha(S) = 1\) for every player \(i\) — think of \(\alpha(S)\) as the fraction of time each member of \(S\) spends in \(S\). The game is balanced if \(\sum_S \alpha(S)\, v(S) \leq v(\mathcal N)\) for every balanced collection.


A TU game has a non-empty core if and only if it is balanced.

The proof is LP duality: the core is non-empty iff the minimum of \(\sum_i x_i\) subject to \(\sum_{i \in S} x_i \geq v(S)\) is at most \(v(\mathcal N)\), and the dual of that LP is the maximisation over balanced weights.

\((\mathcal N, v)\) is convex if \(v(S_1 \cup S_2) + v(S_1 \cap S_2) \geq v(S_1) + v(S_2)\) for all \(S_1, S_2\) — equivalently, a player’s marginal contribution grows with the coalition it joins.

Sufficient conditions for a non-empty core: the game is convex (Shapley, 1971); or it is simple with at least one veto player (give everything to the veto players). In practice one can also try a natural allocation, such as the equal split, and check whether it lies in the core.

title: 15  Coalitions and axiomatic bargaining
text:
15.3 The Shapley value
The core is about stability; the Shapley value is about fairness. Shapley (1953) characterised a unique allocation rule by four axioms: efficiency (\(\sum_i \phi_i = v(\mathcal N)\)), symmetry (interchangeable players get the same), null player (a player contributing nothing to any coalition gets \(0\)), and additivity (\(\phi(v + w) = \phi(v) + \phi(w)\)).

The unique rule satisfying the four axioms is \[\phi_i(v) = \sum_{S \subseteq \mathcal N \setminus \{i\}} \frac{|S|!\,(n - |S| - 1)!}{n!}\,\bigl[v(S \cup \{i\}) - v(S)\bigr],\] player \(i\)’s average marginal contribution over all \(n!\) orders in which the grand coalition can be assembled.


Three players; any coalition containing player 1 and at least one other is worth \(1\); everything else is worth \(0\). Player 1’s marginal contribution is \(1\) whenever he is not first in the order (4 of the 6 orders), so \(\phi_1 = \tfrac23\); players 2 and 3 each contribute only when they join player 1 alone, \(\phi_2 = \phi_3 = \tfrac16\). The core, instead, is \(\{(1, 0, 0)\}\): since \(x_1 + x_2 \geq 1\) and \(x_1 + x_3 \geq 1\) with \(x_1 + x_2 + x_3 = 1\), both \(x_2\) and \(x_3\) must be \(0\). Fairness and stability can disagree. (For convex games the Shapley value always lies in the core.)

Non-superadditive games. When cooperation is not always beneficial (coordination costs, interference, overhead), the grand coalition need not form. The questions become how many coalitions emerge, how they form, and whether the resulting partition is stable. A constructive answer is the merge-and-split process: starting from any partition, coalitions merge if all members benefit, and split if some sub-coalition benefits; under suitable preference orders the process converges to a stable partition.






Applications of coalitional games in ICT include content sharing in P2P networks, spectrum sharing among operators, cooperative transmission and CoMP clustering in cellular networks, vehicular communication, localisation and cooperative crowdsensing.




15.3.1 Two standard families
Power in committees. In a weighted voting game \([q; w_1, \dots, w_n]\) a coalition wins iff its total weight reaches the quota \(q\). The Shapley value of this simple game is the Shapley–Shubik power index: the fraction of orderings in which a player is pivotal, turning a losing coalition into a winning one. Power is not proportional to weight. In \([4; 3, 2, 1, 1]\) the weight-2 player is exactly as powerful as each weight-1 player, since any coalition it makes winning, a weight-1 player would too. The Banzhaf index instead counts, over unordered coalitions, how often a player is critical. A simple game has a non-empty core iff it has veto players, and then the core gives everything to them.
Cost sharing (airport games). Players need a facility of different sizes, with costs \(c_1 \leq c_2 \leq \dots \leq c_n\), and a coalition pays the largest cost among its members, \(C(S) = \max_{i \in S}c_i\). The Shapley value has a transparent form: the cost of each increment \(c_k - c_{k-1}\) is shared equally among the \(n - k + 1\) players who need it, \[\phi_i = \sum_{k=1}^{i}\frac{c_k - c_{k-1}}{n - k + 1}, \qquad c_0 = 0.\] Small users pay only for the part of the runway they use. The same rule is used to share network infrastructure costs.

15.5 Kalai–Smorodinsky solution
Kalai and Smorodinsky (1975) replaced IIA, which they found unappealing, with individual monotonicity: if the feasible set is enlarged in a way that raises the maximum utility attainable by player \(i\), player \(i\) should not lose. Together with axioms 1–4 this characterises the unique solution \[s^{KS} = d + \lambda^* (I - d), \qquad \lambda^* = \max\{\lambda : d + \lambda (I - d) \in S\},\] where \(I = (I_1, I_2)\) is the ideal point of individual maximal utilities. Graphically, \(s^{KS}\) is where the segment from \(d\) to \(I\) meets the Pareto frontier: each player gets the same fraction of their maximal possible gain.
The KS solution extends to more players, asymmetric cases and non-convex \(S\), and rewards most the players with the largest potential gains. Neither solution is “right”: both are points on the Pareto frontier, and the choice between them is philosophical. Constructive procedures that converge to each exist, as do dynamic bargaining models.

Two transmitter–receiver pairs share a frequency-selective channel and interfere with each other. The non-cooperative Nash equilibrium is inefficient: each transmits at full power and beamforms only to maximise its own rate. Using the NE rates as the disagreement point, the NBS (or KS) picks a Pareto-efficient operating point on the rate region — whose shape, not the bargaining formula, is the hard part of the problem. In multimedia transmission the Pareto frontier of a resource-sharing problem is easy to find, but QoE utility functions make the region complex and fairness delicate.

15.6 Exercises
Further problems (not covered by the handbook).

(Weighted voting) Four parties hold weights \(3, 2, 1, 1\) and decisions need \(4\) votes. Compute the Shapley–Shubik and Banzhaf indices and decide whether the core is non-empty.


Solution. Of the \(24\) orderings, \(A\) (weight 3) is pivotal in \(12\) and each of \(B, C, D\) in \(4\): Shapley–Shubik \((\tfrac12, \tfrac16, \tfrac16, \tfrac16)\). Banzhaf counts: \(A\) is critical in \(6\) coalitions, each other party in \(2\), giving normalised \((\tfrac12, \tfrac16, \tfrac16, \tfrac16)\) here as well. \(B\)’s extra weight buys no power. There is no veto player (\(\{B, C, D\}\) wins without \(A\)), so the core is empty: any allocation leaves some winning coalition with less than \(1\).


(Airport game) Three airlines need runways costing \(1\), \(2\), \(3\); a shared runway must be as long as the largest need. Find the Shapley cost shares and check that they are in the core of the cost game.


Solution. Increment \(1\) is shared by three, increment \(2 - 1\) by two, increment \(3 - 2\) by one: \(\phi = (\tfrac13,\ \tfrac13 + \tfrac12,\ \tfrac13 + \tfrac12 + 1) = (\tfrac13, \tfrac56, \tfrac{11}6)\), summing to \(3\). Core of a cost game: no coalition pays more than its stand-alone cost. \(\{1\}\): \(\tfrac13 \leq 1\); \(\{2\}\): \(\tfrac56 \leq 2\); \(\{3\}\): \(\tfrac{11}6 \leq 3\); \(\{1, 2\}\): \(\tfrac76 \leq 2\); \(\{1, 3\}\): \(\tfrac{13}6 \leq 3\); \(\{2, 3\}\): \(\tfrac83 \leq 3\). In the core: airport games are concave cost games, for which the Shapley value is always in the core.

From the course material:

Three firms can share a facility: \(v(\{i\}) = 0\), \(v(\{i, j\}) = 4\) for every pair, \(v(\mathcal N) = 9\). Is the core non-empty? Compute the Shapley value.


Solution. By symmetry try \(x = (3, 3, 3)\): every pair gets \(6 \geq 4\), so the core is non-empty (it is the set of \(x \geq 0\) summing to \(9\) with every pair getting at least \(4\), i.e. \(x_i \leq 5\)). The game is symmetric, so the Shapley value is \((3, 3, 3)\), in the core. (The game is convex: marginal contributions \(0, 4, 5\) increase with coalition size.)


Two players split one unit with disagreement point \(d = (0.2, 0)\) and linear utilities. Find the Nash bargaining solution and compare it with the Kalai–Smorodinsky solution.


Solution. On the frontier \(s_2 = 1 - s_1\): maximise \((s_1 - 0.2)(1 - s_1)\), giving \(s_1 = 0.6\), \(s^* = (0.6, 0.4)\): each player gets their disagreement payoff plus half the surplus \(0.8\). Ideal point: \(I_1 = 1\) (with \(s_2 = 0 \geq d_2\)), \(I_2 = 0.8\) (with \(s_1 = 0.2\)). The KS segment \((0.2 + 0.8\lambda, 0.8\lambda)\) meets \(s_1 + s_2 = 1\) at \(\lambda = 0.5\): \(s^{KS} = (0.6, 0.4)\). For this linear frontier the two coincide.
